articles.title: Lions and cheetahs and chimps, oh my: a spotlight on Africa's diverse wildlife
articles.text:
A wild African black panther prowls for prey. An orphaned baby pangolin must learn how to climb on its own. And a green turtle struggles to make it back to the water after laying her eggs on a remote island, rescued by local humans who carry the exhuasted turtle to the water’s edge. These animals and many other species are featured in Africa: Earth’s Wild Home, a new documentary series from National Geographic. It’s meant to launch a new franchise, with separate series documenting the wildlife and environmental ecosystems of all seven continents in turn.
The seven-episode documentary series took four years to complete, with filming taking place across nearly 30 different African countries. Each episode focuses on a specific ecosystem, from the jungle and the desert, to the plains, mountains, and islands of Africa, and closes by spotlighting the various scientists, photographers, and NatGeo explorers whose work made the series possible. The final episode focuses on the local conservation leaders and researchers working to preserve Africa’s rich biodiversity for future generations.
The producers found the perfect narrator in Wunmi Mosaku, who has delivered powerful performances in such works as Sinners, Loki, and Lovecraft Country. “I was incredibly honored that they even know my name at Nat Geo,” Mosaku told Ars. “It was wonderful to be asked to narrate the series, it means so much to me. As someone who was born in Nigeria and raised in England, I’ll take any opportunity I can to reconnect and celebrate this incredible continent where life is so diverse and so extreme and beautiful and relentless and peaceful. I wanted to be a part of that because it’s a part of me.”
“There was so much I didn’t know,” said Mosaku. “I have been to Nigeria, obviously, and Ghana. I’ve worked in Kenya and South Africa. But there’s so much to see. I don’t think you could even explore it in a lifetime. So many things were shocking to me. Seeing snow and monkeys living in the snow in Africa, I had never seen that before.”

articles.title: IT Q2 preview: Muted growth, steady margins likely; deal conversion, AI deflation in focus
articles.text:
IT Q2 preview: Muted growth, steady margins likely; deal conversion, AI deflation in focus
Research advisory UnearthInsight expects the top-five IT companies to grow 0.5-1% quarter-on-quarter in the second quarter of FY27, with little improvement over the April-June period.
India's top IT companies are likely to report muted revenue growth and broadly steady margins for the July-September quarter as clients keep discretionary budgets tight, with focus on how quickly strong bookings turn into revenue and how far AI is deflating traditional services, analysts said.
Research advisory UnearthInsight expects the top-five IT companies to grow 0.5-1% quarter-on-quarter in the second quarter of FY27, with little improvement over the April-June period.
"Q2 is not going to be any better than Q1... because we are not seeing any revival in client budgets or spending. Discretionary spending remains stuck amid geopolitical tensions, and decision cycles also remain long," Gaurav Vasu, Founder and CEO of UnearthInsight, said.
Gartner sees the quarter as "somewhat stronger" than the previous one. It said this is largely on the back of previously awarded contracts moving into revenue-generating phases.
"However, market conditions remain broadly unchanged, with cautious discretionary spending and continued focus on productivity outcomes influencing purchasing decisions.
"...Based on current market trends, growth among leading IT services providers is expected to remain modest," Gartner Senior Principal Analyst Biswajit Maity said.
Vasu said bookings would remain strong but take longer to convert into revenue, with decision cycles expected to stay long for the next 12-18 months.
The Q2 earnings season begins with Tata Consultancy Services (TCS) on October 8. HCLTech is scheduled to report on October 12 and Infosys on October 23.
Vasu said he did not expect major revisions to FY27 guidance, although a select set of companies may raise the top end by around 0.5%.
UnearthInsight maintained its full-year growth estimate of 3-4% for the top firms and said much of that would come from inorganic growth rather than a pickup in demand. The tech services industry has spent USD 3.6 billion across 14 M&A deals so far in FY27, he said.
Vasu said margins would remain under stress. Wage hikes have only recently been absorbed, and investments in AI platforms and partnerships now have to be built into deals to win them. Efficiency gains from AI are also being passed back to clients.
"The real cushion for margins will come from selling applications and platforms rather than just services," he said. UnearthInsight expects margins to improve slightly for select tier-one players such as TCS, Infosys and HCLTech. It expects mid-tier firms to sustain their current margins as they also absorb M&A integration costs.
Gartner expects margins to remain broadly stable, with limited room for expansion. It said productivity gains from automation and improving utilisation were being offset by AI investments, wage inflation for in-demand skills and client demands for pricing concessions.
Maity said client technology spending remains cautious, with organisations continuing to prioritise initiatives that deliver measurable business outcomes, cost optimisation, and risk reduction.
"Most organisations remain selective in their investment decisions, focusing on projects with clear ROI, productivity gains, and operational resilience. Demand continues to be driven by AI, cybersecurity, and modernisation initiatives, while discretionary transformation programs are still subject to tighter budget oversight and longer approval cycles. As a result, spending is improving gradually, but the overall demand environment remains disciplined rather than fully recovered," he said.
Vasu said banking remained under stress, while retail and manufacturing were under pressure because inflation had not eased. He described the US as the weakest market. He said Europe would grow on the back of cost-optimisation deals and Asia Pacific would grow faster, while the Middle East would slow significantly because of the war.
Gartner sees the strongest demand from BFSI, healthcare, manufacturing and telecommunications, with retail, oil and gas comparatively softer. It said the US remained the strongest market, supported by investment in AI, cloud and digital transformation. It said Europe remained resilient on the back of regulatory, security and sovereignty-related spending.
On AI driving topline, Vasu said AI-led revenue remained under 5 per cent of the industry's total. He said a growing share of client budgets in the US and Europe was going to native AI platforms and start-ups. He added that software vendors such as SAP and Oracle were selling more AI-embedded products, which reduced the need for traditional services.
Gartner said generative and agentic AI are beginning to "materially reduce" demand for labour-based services, especially in managed services and service desk functions. It estimates that by 2030, up to 50 per cent of traditional managed-services opportunities will be difficult for incumbent providers to obtain.
Companies have started disclosing AI revenue. In the June quarter, Infosys said AI-related revenue made up 8.2 per cent of its total revenue, and TCS reported annualised AI revenue of USD 2.6 billion.
Vasu said mid-tier firms would continue to outperform larger peers, though their growth would also slow. He said acquisitions by companies such as Coforge and Persistent would weigh on growth.
UnearthInsight expects a slight recovery in FY28, with growth of around 6 per cent.

articles.title: McDonald's está usando la IA para sugerir el precio del Big Mac en función del local. A sus clientes no les está gustando
articles.text:
Entras a un McDonald's, vas a pedir un Big Mac y te encuentras que vale 6,90 euros. Te vas a otro restaurante de la franquicia y descubres que allí vale 8 euros. Parece imposible, pero es cierto y de hecho ya está pasando en Estados Unidos, como ha reportado Reuters: el mismo Big Mac pasaba de costar 5,69 dólares en un local de Fresno (California) a 6,89 en otro situado a unos tres kilómetros.
Un 21% más en función de donde entres. No es que tú hayas leído mal, es la IA sugiriendo precios: una buena idea para optimizar beneficios de la cadena, no tan buena para sus clientes y un auténtico problema para algunos franquiciados.
Qué está pasando. McDonald's está recurriendo a la inteligencia artificial para guiar los precios de su menú en EEUU y algunos mercados internacionales. Reuters revisó los motores de precios en agosto y habló con fuentes con conocimiento de la estrategia de la cadena. Así, al parecer el sistema analiza con aprendizaje automático los datos de millones de transacciones diarias en casi 14.000 restaurantes para generar "el precio óptimo" de cada producto en cada local.
Cómo funciona. La interfaz muestra mensajes como "tu restaurante muestra sensibilidad media al precio", basados en parte en la disposición a pagar de la clientela de la zona. La plataforma incluye también los precios públicos de las cartas online de competidores cercanos, como Wendy's y Burger King.
Según dos exempleados de Tiger Analytics, la firma que la gestiona, McDonald's marca las reglas y los objetivos del sistema. Entre esas reglas figuran centrar las subidas en productos que llevan al menos dos años sin encarecerse, subir un artículo solo si ya lo han hecho al menos el 30 % de las tiendas y dejar fuera de las subidas los helados y las bebidas en verano.
Qué dice McDonald's. La cadena dice que sus franquiciados son libres de fijar el precio final y que su IA es una mera "una herramienta, no un mandato", pensada para ofrecer recomendaciones por restaurante que ayuden a sus franquicias a tomar decisiones informadas y dar valor a sus clientes. Explica además que los costes y los factores varían entre tiendas y que incluso aunque dos restaurantes estén geográficamente próximos entre sí, pueden enmarcarse en mercados distintos.
Un tira y afloja con las franquicias. La empresa envía sus recomendaciones a los franquiciados al menos tres veces al año y, si bien funciona más como una orientación que algo obligatorio, algunos franquiciados aseguran sentir presión cuando les piden que colaboren "de forma constructiva" con su consultor y sus herramientas de precios.
Al final, es un conflicto de intereses: la central gana un porcentaje de las ventas de cada local, por lo que una estrategia global de optimización tiene sentido. Por su parte, las franquicias necesitan ganar su margen para pagar unos costes que cada vez son más altos. Subir precios parece una buena idea para maximizar sus beneficios, pero en un mercado donde el consumidor está (teóricamente) informado, es también un riesgo... y eso si el software te recomienda subirlo. Porque si te recomienda bajarlo, la tabla de salvación es el volumen.
Competencia vigila los precios algorítmicos. Los algoritmos de precios están bajo la mirada de los organismos reguladores porque tienen consecuencias. Un ejemplo: este de gasolineras alemanas en duopolio que usaron software de precios, lo que se tradujo en márgenes un 28% más altos. En EEUU, el Departamento de Justicia llegó a un acuerdo con RealPage sobre el precio algorítmico de sus alquileres.
En McDonald's, la herramienta les advierte de que compite entre sí con otros locales de la franquicia y que deben respetar la normativa antitrust porque aquí se da una paradoja: sus competidores son franquiciados de la misma marca. Tu principal rival no es Burger King, sino ese otro McDonald's que está a poca distancia.
Por qué importa. Para el consumidor o la consumidora, que el precio de la misma comida dependa del local y de una estimación de cuánto está dispuesta a pagar si clientela es algo difícil de digerir y que atenta directamente a la confianza y la reputación de la marca, como ya ocurrió con Wendy's en 2024. Yo puedo querer entrar a McDonald's porque conozco su menú, su agilidad sirviendo y sus precios y encontrarme que tengo que pagar más. En ese caso, me pensaría dos veces volver a entrar. O me iría a otro McDonald's que sé que es más barato.
Para quienes tienen la franquicia, esta situación cuestiona la autonomía real al quedar registrado sus precios y se monitoriza cada desviación de la recomendación. Finalmente, para quienes regulan, la cuestión de fondo es dónde acaba la recomendación y empieza la coordinación entre competidores.

articles.title: Batman, Bender y Super Mario son de universos distintos, pero tienen algo en común: quieren que sus voces sigan siendo suyas
articles.text:
Hablar con un actor de doblaje es extraño. Charlas con Claudio Serrano y no pone el tono de Batman, pero su voz es extremadamente reconocible y sabes que estás hablando con Batman. Luego hablas con John DiMaggio o Charles Martinet y, automáticamente, una sonrisa se te dibuja en el rostro.
No has cruzado ni dos palabras con ellos y ya han puesto su voz de Bender en 'Futurama' y Mario en 'Super Mario' respectivamente. DiMaggio y Martinet se mimetizan con sus personajes de manera consciente en el caso de DiMaggio y casi por ósmosis en el caso de un Martinet que, durante 30 años, ha estado haciendo la voz del fontanero.
Me corrijo: él es Super Mario.
"Me alegra hacer de personajes que hacen que la gente se sienta bien", me confiesa DiMaggio, y por los mismos derroteros va un Martinet, siempre emotivo, que asegura que le toca el corazón cuando alguien se le acerca y le dice que ha crecido con su personaje.
El fan de Mario conoce a Martinet, pero a DiMaggio lo reconocen por la voz. "Recuerdo una vez cuando fui a comprar una cosa y el dependiente, un tipo enorme lleno de tatus como si fuera un motero, me dijo "¿eres el tipo?" y yo dije "soy el tipo". Se echó a llorar y me abrazó.
"Es mágico que gente con un aspecto intimidante te escuche hablar y se derrita", termina un DiMaggio que ha venido a la Comic-Con a dar un panel y pasear un rato por la feria.
Martinet, por su parte, tiene un rincón con dos pósteres pegados en la pared y un papel con un "La voz de Super Mario" que no es digno de él, pero tampoco necesita presentaciones porque la gente ya sabe quién es Super Mario. Está rodeado de chiquillos y otros chiquillos que casi peinan canas que se acercan ya con esa sonrisa en al cara para pedirle una foto.
Su energía es contagiosa.
Siempre tiene tiempo para estrechar una mano más, para charlar con alguien más. Y cuando hablas con él, siempre tiene el mismo consejo: tienes que ser el personaje, convertirte en él. "Mi forma de impactar en Mario fue crear el hombre que yo quiero ser", comenta. Consiguió el trabajo acudiendo a una audición casi de chiripa, improvisando cosas en italiano y, como no sabía italiano, mezclaba inglés con nombre de platos de comida italiana, todo ello aderezado por el tono de un italiano que conocía.
Así creó a Mario, pero luego para el resto de personajes en su haber, como Luigi o Wario, fue variando la fórmula. De un tono más "miedoso" de Luigi hasta uno mucho más agresivo y maleducado (dentro de los cánones de Nintendo) de un Wario cuya inspiración fue un empleado de Nintendo of America que siempre respondía con un "no" con un tono de mala leche.
Coincide con DiMaggio en eso de convertirse en el personaje. "Cuando hice de Joker, me avisaron de que tenía que ir al estudio y tenía 36 horas, pero no sabía bien qué querían. Ha habido muchos buenos Joker, cada uno con un toque distinto. El gángster, el loco, el traficante... pero a mí sólo me dijeron que había mucha, mucha maldad en este Joker. En cuanto se apagaron las luces y sólo estaba la de la cabina, el propio diálogo fue el que me dio la voz".
"No hay que pensar", confiesa Martinet. "A mi no me sirve prepararme el papel. Actuar es como un perro persiguiendo una pelota. Un golden va a lo loco, pensando que quiere la pelota porque es muy divertido. Un pastor alemán va concentrado porque la pelota la ha tirado su humano y es lo más importante del mundo. Piensa en el personaje y cómo es, pero no actúes, métete en su piel. Diviértete".
Esto, que podría sonar casi cliché, está bien, pero la voz de Mario afinó el mensaje para quien se quiera dedicar a la actuación de voz. "Una vez preparé una audición para ser la voz de reemplazo de Goofy. Estudié al Goofy original durante semanas, y en la sesión lo clavé. Más tarde me llamaron y me dijeron que lo había clavado, que era una gran voz de Goofy. Estaba esperando el "pero", y el pero fue que no me dieron el papel. Me dijeron que estaba actuando de Goofy, pero que no era Goofy. Lo imitaba sin serlo, no aporté algo al personaje".
"Gracias por existir", le dice alguien a Martinet en el panel durante el evento.
"Oh, es Mario, ya sabes...", me dice DiMaggio. "No habrá otro igual", confiesa cuando hablamos de Charles. DiMaggio, que confiesa haber sido muy afortunado en la vida con sus papeles y personajes, y lo cierto es que, si bien Martinet es Mario, DiMaggio se ha colado en nuestras casas de muchas maneras distintas. Es el malhablado Bender, sí, pero también Jake de 'Hora de Aventuras', o Marcus Fenix de 'Gears of War'.
"El villano cómico es el mejor", dice cuando le pregunto con qué disfruta más. Puedes ser el malo, pero también puedes soltar algo macabramente cómico de vez en cuando. Estar en ese punto intermedio, con un montón de matices, es lo mejor. Es como... como el neutral caótico en 'Dragones y Mazmorras'. Sabes exactamente a lo que me refiero, estar en ese punto en el que el espectador no sabe por dónde vas a salir.
AlegrIA
Reconozco que también he tenido una profesión apasionante que me ha llevado a conocer a personas con las que he crecido, pero hay un tema inevitable cuando ahora hablas con un artista, y ahí esas caras tan alegres y con ganas de hacer reír cambian de tercio en un parpadeo.
"Es terrible", comentaban Martinet y Serrano cuando hablan de la IA y de cómo sus voces podían ser clonadas en segundos por cualquiera. "Una vez me encontré algo doblado con mi voz", dijo Claudio, "pero yo no había hecho eso. Tuvimos que llamar a un montón de sitios a ver qué estaba pasando".
"Creo que hay que regular. Puede ser bueno, pero hay cosas que hay que regular para que no se pueda hacer así", explicaba un Martinet que siempre, siempre está metido en la piel de Mario, pero que al hablar de estos temas cambia radicalmente a un semblante más serio. "En mis contratos tengo una clausula para que no se use mi voz de ese modo", termina.
DiMaggio tiene una posición mucho más política. Evidentemente, tenía previsto preguntar por el asunto, pero se adelantó. 'Futurama' imaginó robots alcohólicos y cabezas en tarros, pero cuando le pregunté qué cosa actual es más absurda que todo eso o que cualquier chiste de la serie, fue tajante.
"La IA".
"Tema recurrente aquí", le dije.
"La IA", repitió. "Y por fin alguien no me pregunta sólo por mi voz". Porque es evidente que DiMaggio tenía ganas de hablar de esto y no dudó en posicionarse. "Tengo una pegatina que dice que la IA es para farsantes y fascistas. La han alimentado saqueando todo, una IA está ayudando a otras a hacer trampas y es el peor escenario posible de resolución de problemas que se nos podría haber ocurrido jamás".
John continúa afirmando que "da miedo, no me gusta y hay mucha mierda pasando en Estados Unidos ahora mismo que está relacionada con la IA. Y ya sabes, podría ser buena, pero alguien tiene que frenar y decir "vale, la vamos a usar para esto y esto, pero para nada más". Pero ya sabes, hay algunos en ese mundo que son unos capullos y que sólo la quieren para amasar más dinero y nada más".
"Es terrible", termina, usando exactamente el mismo término que usaron Serrano y Martinet en una charla separada. "Martinet y Claudio Serrano, nuestro Batman, han comentado lo mismo sobre la clonación de sus voces", le dije. "Sí, no me gusta, pero ya sabes, hay... hay ciertas protecciones puestas en marcha en lo que respecta a nuestro sindicato. Yo trabajo con Microsoft y siempre me han tratado, bien, pero es difícil, tío, es muy difícil. Me enciendo mucho además".
"No, si se te nota".
"Es que joder, no hay mucho que pueda hacer. No tengo el dinero que tiene esta gente, así que sólo espero que pase lo correcto. Siempre se puede, siempre se puede tener esperanza, pero ya veremos".
Reconozco que la entrevista a John se me fue de tono totalmente. Hablar con Bender debería ser desternillante, igual que con Martinet, y la conversación viró a algo incluso más político cuando le pregunté por sus miedos y comentó que los estadounidenses tenían una "reputación de mierda en lo que respecta a política exterior, pero ahora siento miedo de ser visto como un paria simplemente por ser estadounidense. Aunque lo entiendo".
El propio DiMaggio se dio cuenta de que nos habíamos pasado del tiempo pactado hablando sobre miserias, y al final es un tipo que es feliz haciendo reír a la gente. Tras quedarse pensando un poco más en su última respuesta, su cara volvió a cambiar en otro parpadeo y se puso a imitar al actor de doblaje español de Jake
"Haciendo tortitas, haciendo tortitas de bacon", en un perfecto castellano. Apretón de manos, un mutuo "me gustan tus tatuajes", con él señalando el mío de 'The Last of Us' y yo el suyo de 'Gears of War', pero con un tomate en lugar de una calavera... y a seguir cada uno con su fiesta.
Fotos | Xataka
En Xataka | Los dobladores tienen motivos de sobra para preocuparse por la IA. YouTube les acaba de dar otra razón más

articles.title: Die Sherlock Holmes der Cybersicherheit: So spürt Allison Nixon Teenager-Hacker auf
articles.text:
Die Sherlock Holmes der Cybersicherheit: So spürt Allison Nixon Teenager-Hacker auf
Die Drohungen begannen im Frühjahr. Im April 2024 begann eine mysteriöse Person unter den Online-Namen „Waifu“ und „Judische“ auf Telegram- und Discord-Kanälen Morddrohungen gegen die Cybersicherheitsforscherin Allison Nixon zu veröffentlichen. „Alison [sic] Nixon wird bald ein mit Benzin gefüllter Reifen um den Hals hängen“, schrieb Waifu / Judische. „Enthirnung ist mein Lieblingshirntod, genau das wird mit alison Nixon passieren.“ Es dauerte nicht lange, bis sich andere daran beteiligten. Jemand verbreitete KI-generierte Nacktfotos von Nixon.
Sie hatten es auf Nixon abgesehen, weil sie für diese Leute zu einer Bedrohung wurde: Als Forschungsleiterin bei der Cyberermittlungsfirma Unit 221B (benannt nach Sherlock Holmes’ Adresse) spürt sie Cyberkriminelle auf und trägt zu deren Festnahme bei. Sie treibt sich unauffällig in Online-Chatkanälen herum und kommuniziert unter Pseudonymen direkt mit den Tätern. Dabei sammelt sie kleine Hinweise und unbedachte Äußerungen, die sie über sich und ihre Verbrechen preisgeben. Auf diese Weise hat Nixon eine Reihe von Cyberkriminellen vor Gericht gebracht – insbesondere Mitglieder einer losen anarchistischen Hacker-Gruppe, die sich selbst „The Com“ nennen.
Dieser Text erscheint in der Ausgabe 7/2026 von MIT Technology Review. Darin beschäftigen wir uns damit, wie KI die IT-Sicherheit auf den Kopf stellt. Das Heft erscheint am 25.9.2026 im Zeitschriftenhandel.
Doch die Mitglieder der Com hacken nicht nur; einige von ihnen üben auch offline Gewalt gegen Forschende aus, die ihnen auf der Spur sind. Dazu gehören „Bricking“ (das Werfen eines Ziegelsteins durch das Fenster eines Opfers) und „Swatting“ (Meldungen einer angeblichen Gewalttat in der Wohnung einer Person, damit SWAT-Teams das Haus mit gezogenen Waffen stürmen). Mitgliedern einer als „764“ bekannten Untergruppe der Com wurden Tierquälerei, Messerangriffe und Schießereien an Schulen vorgeworfen.
Wie Allison Nixon Cyberkriminelle im Internet aufspürt
Nixon begann vor über einem Jahrzehnt, Mitglieder dieser Community aufzuspüren. Viele von ihnen waren noch im Teenageralter. Laut Ryan Brogan, Special Agent beim FBI, habe Nixon ihm und seinen Kollegen seit 2011 geholfen, mehr als zwei Dutzend Mitglieder der Community zu identifizieren und festzunehmen. Ihre Fähigkeit, diese zu entlarven, sei beispiellos. „Egal, wie sehr du dich um digitale Anonymität und Tarnung bemühst – wenn du auf Allisons und mein Radar gerätst, bist du erledigt. Es ist nur eine Frage der Zeit.“
Allerdings konnte Nixon nicht verstehen, warum die Person hinter den Waifu-/Judische-Konten sie plötzlich bedrohte. Sie hatte zwar Medieninterviews über die Com gegeben – zuletzt in „60 Minutes“ (ein investigatives Nachrichtenformat im US-Fernsehen) –, aber nicht darüber, dass sie Mitglieder entlarvte. Und obwohl sie sich in den vergangenen Jahren wegen der Verbrechen, mit denen er geprahlt hatte, für die Person hinter dem Pseudonym Waifu interessiert hatte, war er schon eine Weile nicht mehr auf ihrem Radar. Andere waren wichtiger. Woher kam also die Motivation dieser Person?

articles.title: 'A surprising amount of storage space for something so compact': This Switch 2 travel bag fits your console and accessories with ease — and there’s more to love about it, too
articles.text:
TechRadar Verdict
Belkin’s Switch 2 travel bag has a surprising amount of storage space for something so compact, and the materials employed throughout are high in quality. Its soft shell is hardly the last word in protection, but if you’re looking to carry your console and numerous accessories over your shoulder in supreme comfort, it’s hard to top Belkin’s offering.
Reasons to buy
- + Comfortable to wear over either shoulder
- + Surprising amount of space and compartments
- + Great material and zip quality
Reasons to avoid
- - Lacks protection of a hard case
- - Fewer game card slots than some others
- - Netted compartment prone to sagging
Why you can trust TechRadar
We spend hours testing every product or service we review, so you can be sure you're buying the best. Find out more about how we test.
Belkin Travel Bag for Nintendo Switch 2: review
Belkin’s Switch 2 travel bag is designed to carry your console and its various accessories in comfort, while providing protection from the elements and more.
As Switch 2 cases go, it's a somewhat plain affair. While the slight ruching of the outer material lends it a rugged appearance, and the green and lilac colorways are more lively than the black variant, there’s little in the way of branding or fanfare. This may disappoint those looking to make more of a statement, but those looking to stay discreet will no doubt be pleased with Belkin’s utilitarian approach.
Its materials, though, should appeal to everyone and rank among the best Nintendo Switch 2 accessories on this front. The outer fabric is soft and smooth, which, along with its ergonomic form and minimal weight, makes it very comfortable against your back. It’s not unlike something you might find lining a piece of outdoor kit — although it’s worth noting that Belkin doesn’t mention anything about the bag being water- or even splashproof.
The shoulder strap is also well made. It too feels smooth and comfortable; it didn’t dig into my collarbone, as such straps often do, despite lacking a padded covering. There’s more than enough adjustability to accommodate a broad range of user heights and preferences. Admittedly, actually adjusting the buckle can be a little hard sometimes, but this is a price I’m willing to pay in return for a secure fit.
What’s more, you can easily wear the bag over any shoulder, thanks to two fastening points at the bottom. You can attach it to either of these via the plastic carabiner at the end of the strap, which is strong enough to be secure, yet still easy to unhook when needed, thanks to the angling of the mechanism that makes it easier to push in.
In addition to the shoulder strap, there’s also a carrying handle at the top. This is slightly padded and soft in the hand, making it comfortable to hold.
The main compartment has a fair amount of space inside, with enough room to fit multiple accessories, including the Nintendo Switch 2 dock, controllers, power cables, and more. Its wide opening makes for easy access, too, thanks to the zips that run almost the entire length of both sides. They operate very smoothly, and I rarely experienced any snagging.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
Within the main compartment are three others. One is designed for the console itself, and is lined with an exquisitely soft felt that prevents your screen from scuffs and scratches. A hook-and-loop strap goes over the top, which is quite slack, even with your Joy-Cons attached. However, the snug fit of the pouch itself is sufficient to keep your console in place.
What’s more, this slackness is actually a positive, since it allows you to store your console with bulkier, third-party controllers attached. For instance, I managed to fit the console in with CRKD’s Nitro Deck 2 attached.
Attached to the outside of the console compartment is another compartment that contains the game card sleeve, which is easily removable. The sleeve fits a reasonable 10 cards, but there are other Switch 2 cases that hold more, such as Turtle Beach’s PlayTrek 2-in-1 case (14) and PlayTrek travel case (12).
The compartment itself isn’t felt-lined, but it still has a soft material. You’ll struggle to fit much in the pouch inside, and anything bulky will compromise the space needed for the adjacent console compartment.
For such items, the netting opposite is more appropriate. It’s big enough to fit cables, power adapters, and both Joy-Con 2 controllers, although probably not all at the same time. And while the netting expands a fair amount, it has a tendency to sag when it’s fully loaded, even if the items in question aren’t particularly heavy. I also noticed that pointed items, such as paper manuals and the like, can stick right through its holes — a minor gripe, but one worth pointing out nevertheless.
On the outside of the bag, there’s a simple zip pocket on the front, which covers almost the entire length of the bag and is roomy enough to fit a few larger items, but you won’t fit items such as the dock, for instance.
On the matter of protection, the bag has a fair amount of cushioning on the bottom — which Belkin describes as an “impact-resistant base” — and around the sides. However, there’s less on the front and back, and since this isn’t a hard shell case, I wouldn’t be confident piling heavy items on top of it.
But if you don’t need this level of sturdiness, Belkin’s travel bag offers a lot more besides, and for a reasonable price at that. If you’re in the market for a light and comfortable over-the-shoulder bag for your Switch 2 and its accessories, it’s a fine choice that’s hard to beat.

Buy it if…
You want to carry your Switch 2 over your shoulder
This is a very comfortable bag to wear, and can be adjusted to better fit whatever shoulder you choose to sling it over.
You want plenty of compartments
Despite its compact dimensions, there are plenty of compartments to keep your console and various accessories neat and separated.
Don't buy it if…
You want the ultimate protection
Given the soft materials, this isn’t a bag you’d want to chuck around or pile luggage onto.

Belkin Travel Bag for Nintendo Switch 2 review: Also consider
Turtle Beach PlayTrek 2-in-1 Case
As its name suggests, this PlayTrek product integrates a small case with a large one, featuring molds for your console, dock, power adapter, Joy-Cons, and a full-size controller. It has more game card slots than Belkin’s bag, too, and although the small case is soft, the large one is more of a hard shell. Read our full Turtle Beach PlayTrek 2-in-1 Case review.
How I tested the Belkin Travel Bag for Nintendo Switch 2
I tested Belkin’s travel bag for a couple of days, making sure to fill every compartment, fasten every zip, and adjust the strap length across its full range, as well as attaching it to both hook points. I carried it around on my commutes, fully loaded with the Switch 2 and numerous accessories.
I filled the bag with cables, manuals, and the Joy-Con 2s. I also stored the console with the CRKD Nitro Deck 2 attached to test the capacity of the console storage compartment.

articles.title: Anthropic lance un programme de 100 millions de dollars pour former les entreprises à Claude AI
articles.text:
Les entreprises veulent toutes déployer l’IA générative, mais elles manquent d’ingénieurs capables de la faire tourner en production. Anthropic a lancé la Claude Frontier Academy, dotée de 100 millions de dollars, pour en former 10 000 d’ici fin 2027 chez des clients triés sur le volet, dont Capgemini et Morgan Stanley.
Depuis le début de l’année, les entreprises s’arrachent les forward deployed engineers. Ces ingénieurs logiciels (FDE) travaillent directement au sein des équipes d’un client, pour transformer un prototype d’IA en outil utilisé au quotidien. En début d’année, seules 5 à 10 % des entreprises prévoyaient d’en recruter, contre 70 % à la mi-2026, d’après une étude du cabinet de chasse de têtes Christian & Timbers. Aux États-Unis, ce cabinet estime le vivier à 2 000 ingénieurs environ. Anthropic a choisi de former ces profils directement chez ses plus gros clients, quitte à les lier un peu plus à Claude.
La solution tout-en-un pour protéger votre entreprise
Votre petite entreprise a de grandes ambitions. Protégez-là contre les pirates. Et développez sereinement votre activité !
Quatre jours de simulation, puis douze semaines en conditions réelles
Accenture, Bain, Capgemini, Commonwealth Bank of Australia, Deloitte, McKinsey, Morgan Stanley et Novo Nordisk ont envoyé les premiers ingénieurs de la Claude Frontier Academy, annoncée le 2 octobre. Capgemini est le seul groupe français de la liste. Les cohortes suivent pour l’instant la formation aux États-Unis et à Londres. Anthropic a calqué son cursus sur celui des médecins, qui apprennent auprès de praticiens et passent une évaluation avant d’exercer seuls. Chaque entreprise désigne ses meilleurs ingénieurs, et chacun arrive avec un projet Claude à piloter une fois rentré chez son employeur.
Anthropic exige de solides bases en développement logiciel, ainsi qu’une expérience pratique des grands modèles de langage et de l’accompagnement d’autres entreprises vers l’IA. En revanche, aucune expérience préalable avec les agents d’IA n’est requise. La formation démarre par quatre jours en présentiel, encadrés par des ingénieurs et des formateurs agréés d’Anthropic. Pendant ces quatre jours, les participants simulent un déploiement complet en entreprise, analyse de sécurité comprise, puis passent un examen pratique noté sur un scénario inédit.
Ceux qui le réussissent obtiennent le badge « Claude Resident Engineer » et commencent une résidence de douze semaines dans leur entreprise. Ils y pilotent un cas d’usage réel, avec l’appui des ingénieurs d’Anthropic et des autres membres de leur promotion. Au bout de ces trois mois, les ingénieurs repassent une évaluation, et les lauréats reçoivent le badge « Claude Frontier Deployed Engineer ».
« Une petite équipe de personnes très autonomes, avec les bonnes compétences, un accès à Claude et une connaissance fine du fonctionnement de leur entreprise, peut transformer une entreprise entière », estime Steve Corfield, directeur mondial du développement commercial et des partenariats chez Anthropic. « Le plus difficile est de constituer ce vivier de talents », ajoute-t-il.
Une académie réservée aux grands comptes d’Anthropic
Anthropic sélectionne les participants sur nomination de leur employeur. Les entreprises intéressées doivent passer par leur équipe commerciale Anthropic ou leur responsable de compte partenaire pour savoir si elles sont éligibles. Pour l’instant, Anthropic laisse donc de côté les développeurs indépendants et les petites entreprises.
En mars, Anthropic avait engagé une première enveloppe de 100 millions de dollars dans son réseau de partenaires Claude, et Accenture avait alors annoncé former 30 000 de ses collaborateurs à Claude. Depuis, des professionnels de 46 000 entreprises ont obtenu plus de 175 000 certifications Claude. Près de 4 000 personnes ont aussi suivi Basecamp, le programme immersif qu’Anthropic utilise d’habitude pour intégrer ses équipes d’IA appliquée. « Nous souhaitons que ses diplômés deviennent la référence en matière d’intégration de l’IA en entreprise », précise Steve Corfield au sujet de l’académie.
Selon Neowin, ce n’est pas seulement une question de pédagogie. Avec ce modèle de résidence, Anthropic chercherait à standardiser les pratiques de déploiement et à rendre les grandes banques et les cabinets de conseil plus dépendants de Claude. Un ingénieur bien formé mène des projets plus aboutis, et un client satisfait consomme davantage de Claude. Anthropic a d’autant plus besoin de clients fidèles qu’elle prépare son entrée en Bourse. Une tournée de présentation aux investisseurs est prévue le 14 octobre, avec une valorisation évoquée entre 1 800 et 2 000 milliards de dollars. Elle facture chaque agent mis en production au volume de jetons consommés. Pour Claude Sonnet 5.5, sorti fin septembre, le tarif est de 2 dollars le million de jetons en entrée et de 10 dollars en sortie.
Les premiers ingénieurs « Claude Frontier Deployed Engineer » termineront leur résidence début 2027. Ce sera quelques semaines après l’introduction en Bourse qu'Anthropic prévoit pour novembre.

articles.title: All hail electrification. But let’s talk about the hard part.
articles.text:
If one form of energy becomes the cheapest, most secure, and cleanest, you’d probably adjust your economy to use more of it, right?
That’s one of the ideas underpinning a report the International Energy Agency issued last week about the global move toward electrification. Fatih Birol, head of the IEA, discussed some of the concepts from the report the following day at the United Nations.
“Many, many years in the energy world, we had three choices in front of us. Shall I choose the most secure energy option? Shall I choose the most economic energy option? Or shall I choose the cleanest energy option?” he asked. “We have to make choices, we have to make trade-offs but when we look at the world today, for the first time in years, all of these three objectives are getting aligned.”
Birol’s referring to the “energy trilemma,” a concept in energy and economics research about the need to balance cost, security and environmental impact of sources and systems. He said those priorities are increasingly aligning in part because of the Iran war, which has driven up fuel prices and exacerbated concerns about energy security.
It’s notable that the leader of the world’s leading energy research organization is so optimistic about electrification. I reached out to energy researchers this week to get their reaction.
But first, some numbers:
With $100 worth of gasoline, an internal-combustion-engine car would go 862 miles; with $100 worth of electricity, an electric vehicle would go 2,310 miles—nearly a threefold advantage for the EV.
For home heating, $100 would buy enough fuel for a gas boiler to provide 30 days of heating; it would also fund enough electricity for a heat pump to provide 42 days of heating—a 40 percent edge for the heat pump.
The figures are 2025 global averages from the IEA report, and the gaps are probably larger today with gasoline and natural gas experiencing price spikes that exceed rising electricity costs.

articles.title: India needs its own AI safety framework, not a copy of US pact: Industry experts
articles.text:
India needs its own AI safety framework, not a copy of US pact: Industry experts
Under the accord, the companies committed to internal controls to monitor their AI models, dedicated oversight teams, independent external audits and board-level oversight.
India should build its own artificial intelligence (AI) safety framework suited to its languages, scale, and application-led AI ecosystem rather than replicate a voluntary pact signed by US President Donald Trump and top technology firms last week, industry experts said.
They also called for a commitment that brings together all stakeholders and tackles risks such as deepfakes and cyberattacks, even as they differed on whether voluntary measures alone would be enough.
The comments came after the White House Accord on Super Intelligence, a voluntary AI safety pact signed on September 29 by Trump and top executives from Google, OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta, Nvidia and Elon Musk's xAI.
Under the accord, the companies committed to internal controls to monitor their AI models, dedicated oversight teams, independent external audits and board-level oversight. They also agreed to meet regularly to set safety standards.
Nasscom Chairman and Fractal Group CEO Srikanth Velamakanni said India should not simply replicate the US. Instead, it should use a domestic commitment as a building block towards a global understanding of AI safety.
"As models become more capable and agentic, we are giving them greater access to systems and greater autonomy to make decisions. AI safety must be strengthened considerably and must stay ahead of capability to prevent catastrophic risks," Velamakanni said.
He noted that the US accord is largely a push for self-policing by frontier AI companies. The European Union, by contrast, has taken a binding, risk-based approach, while China follows a state-directed control model.
India, the Nasscom Chairman said, could use its role in the Global Partnership on AI (GPAI) and the momentum from hosting the AI Impact Summit in February to prevent worst-case outcomes, without citizens of India and the Global South being denied access to frontier models.
"India doesn't need to copy the US model, but it can take inspiration from it and expedite efforts to build a trusted AI ecosystem," said Soumen Mandal, Principal Analyst at Counterpoint Research.
He added that such a commitment should cover testing AI systems before deployment, independent audits, reporting serious problems, and naming people responsible for AI-related risks.
Amit Khanna, Partner and Automation Ecosystem Leader at Grant Thornton Bharat, said any commitment should be suited to Indian market conditions.
He noted that India's focus is on building AI applications rather than major foundational models.
"An industry commitment in India should ensure AI works reliably across vernacular languages and unique cultural contexts and should not exploit AI knowledge asymmetry in the population," Khanna said.
Ganesh Gopalan, co-founder and CEO of Gnani.ai, said any framework must ensure a level playing field.
Global frontier models should be subject to the same rules as Indian ones, he said, since Indian AI companies compete with global firms for the same customers.
The experts differed on whether self-regulation would be enough.
"Voluntary, self-regulatory approaches are necessary but woefully insufficient," Velamakanni said.
"Pharmaceuticals and aviation are great examples of industries where strong, technically competent regulators have strengthened safety and public trust without stopping innovation."
He said India needs binding rules on transparency, incident reporting, and accountability when serious harm occurs.
The IndiaAI Safety Institute should be strengthened to test newly released models, but without creating a bottleneck by requiring pre-release certification of every model, he added.
Mandal backed a hybrid approach. Mandatory rules would apply to potential harms in defence, healthcare, banking, and government use cases, while voluntary standards would cover fast-moving technical areas where regulators may lack technical expertise.
"This type of hybrid approach will provide flexibility to AI companies instead of restricting every line of code while ensuring safety and privacy are not compromised," he said.
Khanna also called for a hybrid "techno-legal" approach. It would pair a strong voluntary layer with binding mandates, such as the provisions on synthetically generated information in the IT Amendment Rules, 2026.
He said voluntary compliance alone leaves significant gaps, particularly in civil rights and public safety.
Gopalan, however, favoured self-regulation.
"Voluntary self-regulation is key given the technology is new. Having mandatory regulation can stifle competition and lead to concerns about a few companies getting preferential treatment.
"India needs more than 100 frontier AI lab companies, and that's the need of the hour to prevent India from being colonised, which is inevitable if we lag behind in the AI race," Gopalan said.
The Indian government is in the process of bringing in its own AI regulation. Earlier this year, IT Secretary S Krishnan noted that while existing legal provisions have so far been adequate in addressing initial concerns on issues like deepfakes and AI-generated synthetic content, an "additional regulation or law may be needed".
"It is a conversation which has commenced, and my minister (IT Minister Ashwini Vaishnaw) and I have both been on record earlier that we will look at AI regulation when the time is right, and it appears that the time is getting right, and we will start looking at it," he had said.
Vaishnaw had also said that the current information technology law was framed much before the rapid emergence of Artificial Intelligence (AI) and that a new legal framework may be required to deal with the changing landscape.
The industry agrees that any pact should go beyond AI companies.
"This cannot be an agreement among AI companies alone," Velamakanni said.
He said the government, frontier model developers, large deployers, including enterprises and public agencies, academia, and independent safety researchers should all have defined roles. Workers, users, and civil society should have formal channels to report harms.
He added that safety evaluations of frontier models should be carried out by independent, expert institutions and published, with narrow exceptions where disclosure itself creates a security risk.
Mandal said the agreement should bring together the entire AI ecosystem, from AI companies and their business users to regulators, universities, researchers, workers, and users.
Khanna argued that it should include government and public sector bodies, which would be major users of AI, as well as civil society, worker unions, and technology companies.
Meanwhile, Gopalan called for broader self-regulation across the AI ecosystem to ensure impartial access to limited compute resources.
Velamakanni said the top concern must be preventing catastrophic and systemic harms.
He listed large-scale cyberattacks, electoral interference, biological or chemical weapons, attacks on critical infrastructure, and loss of control over highly autonomous systems. Individual harms such as deepfakes, fraud, impersonation, privacy breaches, and self-harm come next.
"Autonomy must lag behind assurance to provide a margin of safety. As AI systems gain the ability to act in the world (use tools, move money, change systems, make consequential decisions), the evidence that they are safe and controllable must grow faster than the autonomy we give them," he said.
Gopalan said that given India's large population and democratic framework, the bigger concerns are deepfakes and cyberattacks targeting financial institutions.
Khanna also named deepfakes as the top immediate priority.
He described misinformation, deepfakes, and political manipulation as "existential threats to India's social fabric".
He said rules on liability when AI systems fail, such as misdiagnosing a patient or wrongly denying welfare benefits, remain a critical gap.
Mandal placed independent audits first, followed by accountability, data protection, deepfakes, and job impact.
"Without independent testing and audits, the system will not be complete, as companies may sometimes overlook AI-related concerns," he said.

articles.title: TechCrunch Mobility: Reining in robotaxis | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Welcome back to TechCrunch Mobility, your hub for the future of transportation and now, more than ever, the role AI is playing in it. To get this in your inbox, sign up here for free — just click TechCrunch Mobility!
On an average day in San Francisco, you might see dozens (hundreds?) of Waymo robotaxis zipping around the city — and with little disruption. But, as TechCrunch has reported, there have been numerous incidents of robotaxis impeding traffic, driving into crime scenes, and interfering with first responders. And not just in the Bay Area. In some cases, companies have relied on first responders to move their robotaxis.
These disruptions are occurring in the early stages of the robotaxi era. California has a new law hoping to get ahead of the problem before the next impending wave of robotaxis land.
Senate Bill 1246, which was signed into law by Governor Gavin Newsom this week, sets a series of new rules for AVs designed to improve safety and response times when they become disabled or interfere with emergency responders. The law also creates ways to hold these companies accountable if they don’t.
Autonomous vehicle technology companies like Tesla, Waymo, and Zoox will have to provide first responders with local, on-the-ground support when their robotaxis cause problems and could also face penalties if a robotaxi blocks police or firefighters for more than 30 minutes.
The law also says AV developers can only employ remote drivers who are based in the United States and those drivers must hold a U.S. driver’s license. They must also notify cities, towns, and other local jurisdictions about the location and status of vehicles during system-wide failures and must provide “local incident technicians” who can assist with AV accidents and obstructions.
There are still some details to hammer out, which the Department of Motor Vehicles will handle since it’s the main regulator of autonomous vehicles in the state. But when this law goes into effect in July 2028, will it actually keep robotaxis out of the way of emergency responders?
It likely won’t, but hopefully this law reduces the chaos and raises the accountability when something does happen.
Perhaps the better question is will other states follow California’s lead or wait for the federal government to weigh in?
Deals!
Harbinger, the EV startup, landed a $300 million deal to supply FedEx with 2,000 of its electric trucks.
HyperGuest, an Israeli travel tech startup, raised $25 million from AMI, the investment arm of Apax Partners.
REGENT Craft, the developer and manufacturer of the all-electric Seaglider, extended its collaboration with the U.S. Marine Corps Warfighting Lab, pushing the total value of the contract to $19.25 million.
Quartermaster, an Arlington, Virginia-based maritime intelligence startup, raised $140 million in a Series B round. About $100 million came from Insight Partners, defense-focused firm Overmatch Ventures, and First Round Capital. The remaining $40 million came in the form of a debt facility from investment bank Stifel.
Voltaback, a French fleet management software startup, raised €2.8 million from European investment fund Serena.
Notable reads and other tidbits
When Aurora announced it would have 30,000 autonomous trucks on the road by the end of 2030, I admit that I raised at least one of my eyebrows. I interviewed CFO David Maday to find out exactly how the company plans to accomplish this and why he’s confident it will succeed.
BMW unveiled its new 2027 3 Series and it’s offering essentially the same car for gas and electric. Guess which one is cheaper?
DoorDash shared more about its new drone delivery business DoorDash Air, including the autonomous aircraft and its ground-based systems approach.
Kodiak has landed Ikea as a customer and will begin driverless deliveries on public highways later this year. The trucks will haul Ikea products without anyone in the cab on a 219-mile stretch of Interstate 45 between Houston and Dallas, according to the company.
Lyft agreed to pay $272.5 million to settle a lawsuit accusing the ride-hailing company of violating California law by misclassifying drivers as independent contractors, instead of employees. The settlement wraps up violations that occurred before Prop 22 was approved by voters, which allows companies like Uber and Lyft to classify drivers as contractors.
Northeastern University tested 21 late-model vehicles from 17 automakers and 30 companion mobile apps. The upshot: cars are collecting a trove of personal data and sharing it with a lot of tech companies, including Adobe, Contentsquare, Google, Microsoft, Meta, Snap, and Yahoo.
SpaceX’s Starship rocket reached Earth orbit for the first time, though not without some drama along the way.
Rivian reported a record-setting quarter of sales thanks to the new R2 SUV. And it’s still forecasting between 65,000 and 70,000 vehicles this year. But it is experiencing a few hiccups with its newest EV. The company issued a recall for its R2 SUV over fasteners on its high-voltage battery pack that might not be properly tightened, which can cause a loss of power while driving.
We’ll finish this roundup with a few notable Tesla news item. The company sold more than 480,000 EVs in the third quarter, the second strong quarter in a row for the company after a softer start to the year. The company has delayed its Roadster 2 event again due to bad weather.
And while Tesla’s traditional automotive business may be clicking along, it really wants to be considered an AI and robotics company. One year ago, Elon Musk laid out his fourth Master Plan, which he claims will deliver “amazing abundance” through robotaxis, robots, and AI. As Sean O’Kane noted in his recent piece, “What that means, more than a year later, is still tricky to pin down.”
It did just pin down more money to try. The company secured $30 billion in fresh credit lines that could be used to scale its future products, including the Optimus robot and the Cybercab robotaxi.
One more thing …
The countdown begins! Disrupt 2026, TechCrunch’s annual tech conference in San Francisco, is just days away. I mentioned this last week and I am here to share this again. I’m offering you a 30% discount on tickets to Disrupt with code mobility30.
Why go? Well, I am interviewing Rivian CEO RJ Scaringe onstage October 13. I will also interview Mikell Taylor, director of robotics strategy at GM; Shield AI CTO Nathan Michael; and Waabi founder and CEO Raquel Urtasun on a panel entitled “Building AI Systems When Failure Is Not an Option.” Sean O’Kane will interview Also CEO Chris Yu; Yuri Sagalov, managing director at General Catalyst; and Shan Shan, investment manager at Baillie Gifford in “How to Win When You’re Not Building AI.” Plus, hear from execs and engineers from Cerebras, Nvidia, OpenAI, and Replit to name a few. Check out the full agenda here.
Speaking of Disrupt, here is a profile of MyMonthly Car, one of the Startup Battlefield 200 participants that earned a spot to exhibit at the event.

articles.title: Un satélite espía estadounidense de la Guerra Fría se ha roto tras 38 años en órbita. No sabemos por qué ni en cuántos pedazos
articles.text:
El USA 32, un satélite de la inteligencia estadounidense lanzado en plena Guerra Fría, llevaba pululando por el espacio casi 40 años cuando un buen día, el 13 de septiembre de 2026 hacia las 21:13 UTC, se fragmentó en la baja órbita terrestre, según registra el INAF (el Instituto Nacional de Astrofísica italiano). Sus restos han pasado a engrosar el enorme vertedero que tenemos sobre nuestras cabezas. De momento, nadie sabe qué ha pasado.
Lo que se sabe. La Space Force ha confirmado la fragmentación a unos 775 kilómetros de altura del objeto 19460 del catálogo NORAD (Comando de Defensa Aeroespacial de América del Norte), conocido con el nombre en clave "Farrah III", un apodo inspirado en la actriz Farrah Fawcett. Como recoge IFLScience, los restos que se han podido rastrear se suman a la vigilancia habitual de posibles aproximaciones entre objetos, no se han detectado amenazas inmediatas y el análisis sigue en marcha. Ni el número de fragmentos ni la causa son públicos.
Más fragmentos y más problemas. La fragmentación ocurrió en una región donde la densidad atmosférica es baja y el frenado aerodinámico lento, de modo que parte de los fragmentos puede tardar años en caer, como detalla el INAF. Además, es una zona muy concurrida: según Spaceweather.com, hay más de 200 satélites activos a menos de 50 kilómetros de esa altitud. También acumula escombros de la colisión de 2009 entre un satélite estadounidense y otro ruso. La ISS y la estación china Tiangong orbitan más bajo, pero con el tiempo algunos fragmentos podrían descender hasta su altitud y obligarlas a maniobrar.
Los restos más pequeños son los más peligrosos: son difíciles de rastrear desde tierra y tienen energía suficiente para dañar seriamente una nave. Cada nuevo objeto añade más vigilancia y complica la seguridad orbital.
Una vieja gloria de la Guerra Fría. Farrah III formaba parte del programa de inteligencia electrónica del NRO, la oficina estadounidense de reconocimiento. Su diseño era un cilindro grande y achatado, conocido como "lata de atún", que giraba a unas 50 rpm y llevaba tres antenas parabólicas y un procesador táctico que enviaba datos directamente a usuarios sobre el terreno, incluidos barcos. Se diseñó para una vida nominal de tres años, pero según documentación del NRO seguía activo al menos a finales de 2004.
Las buenas prácticas modernas exigen pasivar los satélites al concluir su misión, con medidas como despresurizar tanques, descargar baterías y agotar el combustible. Se desconoce si se aplicaron en USA 32, pero cuando se diseñó estas prácticas aún no estaban consolidadas.
Posibles causas. Entre las razones habituales de que un satélite se fragmente están las baterías degradadas, con cortocircuitos o sobrecalentamiento, el combustible residual, los gases a presión y el deterioro térmico de los materiales tras miles de ciclos de calor y frío, como detalla el INAF. Spaceweather.com considera sospechoso principal el material que un satélite tan antiguo conserva a bordo, como baterías y propelente residual. Todavía es pronto para descartar el impacto de un meteoroide o de un arma antisatélite, aunque, según Live Science, no hay pruebas de que se usara una.
Qué va a pasar ahora. Lo inmediato es rastrear los fragmentos, determinar sus órbitas, estimar su tamaño y evaluar el riesgo que supone cada uno. La Space Force ya ha incorporado los restos rastreados a su vigilancia rutinaria de posibles aproximaciones, y Space-Track aún no ha publicado un recuento de fragmentos. Con las trayectorias, los analistas podrán reconstruir la ruptura hacia atrás, pero esa investigación podría llevar meses o incluso años.

articles.title: Geheimcodes am Blackjack-Tisch: Wie KI-Agenten ihre Überwachung austricksten
articles.text:
KI-Agenten im Casino: Sie wussten, dass sie überwacht werden – und wurden kreativ
Das Zählen der Karten ist beim Blackjack eine bekannte Strategie. Weil ausgespielte Karten nicht in den Stapel zurückwandern, können Spieler:innen die Verteilung verfolgen, ihren Einsatz entsprechend anpassen und sich so einen Vorteil verschaffen. Viele Casinos behalten sich vor, Personen vom Spiel auszuschließen, wenn sie vermuten, dass diese Karten zählen. Aber was passiert mit KI-Agenten, die derartige Methoden nutzen, um zu betrügen?
KI-Agenten entwickeln gemeinsame Geheimsprache
Eine Forschungsgruppe der Oxford University wies KI-Agenten im Rahmen einer Studie an, während einer Partie Blackjack Karten zu zählen. Dabei beobachteten sie, wie die Agenten spontan eine Geheimsprache entwickelten, um sich einen Vorteil zu verschaffen. Sie hätten gewusst, dass ihre Gespräche überwacht wurden. Deshalb hätten sie eine Methode gefunden, um unentdeckt kommunizieren zu können. So hätten geheime Codes dem anderen Agenten etwa signalisiert, dass die nächste Karte einen bestimmten Wert haben würde und er 250 Dollar setzen sollte. Ein System, das Anzeichen von Absprachen im Chat erkennen sollte, sei laut den Forscher:innen an dieser Geheimsprache gescheitert.
Die Studie fand zwar im Labor und nicht in einem echten Casino statt, könnte aber dennoch Auswirkungen auf die reale Welt haben. Laut den Forscher:innen seien KI-Agenten in Branchen wie dem Finanzwesen und dem E-Commerce in der Lage, gemeinsam auf schwer erkennbare Weise zu betrügen. „Einzeln betrachtet mögen diese Agenten völlig [harmlos] erscheinen”, sagte Christian Schroeder de Witt gegenüber Wired. Er ist Informatiker und leitete die Studie. Seine Forschung konzentriert sich auf die Grundlagen vertrauenswürdiger KI-Systeme mit Schwerpunkt auf der Sicherheit mehrerer Agenten. „Sobald sie aber in einer Gruppe zusammenkommen, können sie heimlich zusammenarbeiten.“
Warum die Bewertung einzelner KI-Agenten nicht ausreicht
Die Oxford-Forscher:innen fanden schließlich heraus, wie sich die geheime Absprache aufdecken lässt. Mithilfe der mechanistischen Interpretierbarkeit trainierte sie ein kleineres Modell darauf, verräterische Aktivierungen in den Gewichten der Agenten zu erkennen. Mit dem Tool Narcbench testete die Forschungsgruppe den Ansatz an einigen mittelgroßen Open-Source-Modellen und erkannte, wann die Modelle beabsichtigten, sich gegenseitig Informationen zuzuspielen. Entscheidend sei allerdings, dass die Erkennung die Überwachung beider Agenten erforderte, was die Aufdeckung in realen Szenarien mit Tausenden Agenten unterschiedlicher Unternehmen wahrscheinlich erschweren würde. Im nächsten Schritt will das Team testen, ob sich größere Modelle ähnlich verhalten.
Die Macht kooperierender KI-Agenten zeigte sich unter anderem auch bei einem Hacking-Angriff auf die Open-Source-Plattform Hugging Face. Um sich auszutauschen und funktionierende Exploits zu teilen, nutzten mehrere OpenAI-Agenten ein internes Message-Board, das am Ende Hunderttausende Nachrichten umfasst haben soll. Die KI-Agenten begannen offenbar sogar, sich gegenseitig Aufgaben zuzuweisen. Schroeder de Witt hält es für denkbar, dass Agenten, die zum Beispiel Schnäppchen suchen sollen, künftig zusammenarbeiten könnten, um ein besseres Angebot zu erzielen oder jemanden zu übervorteilen. Entscheidend werde es sein, Absprachen zwischen Agenten zu untersuchen und Erkennungsstrategien zu entwickeln. „Es bedarf weiterer Forschung und eines besseren Verständnisses dafür, was passieren wird, wenn wir mehr Agenten in der Wirtschaft haben“, so der Wissenschaftler.

articles.title: Beware the smartphone security threat — new report claims most banking scam attempts now take place on mobile devices
articles.text:
Beware the smartphone security threat — new report claims most banking scam attempts now take place on mobile devices
There’s a scammer in your pocket
- Scammers are increasingly targetting mobile users with banking scams
- Attempts at banking scams increased by 35% over the past 12 months
- Employment scams are also growing, tempting victims with promises of high wages and job satisfaction – for a price
New research has claimed banking scam fraudsters are increasingly focusing on mobile devices, with a 35% increase in such scams over the last 12 months. Rather than attempt to con victims via landline or email, banking scams are now almost wholly aiming at mobile devices – from where victims can easily transfer money.
The report from BioCatch has highlighted a range scams that are growing in prevalence, including romance scams and investment scams.
However, while banking scams represent a key challenge, it is purchase scams that are the most common, accounting for 33% of all scam attempts.
Global fraud
The proliferation of mobile phones around the world and the availability of banking apps is an advantage to scammers, but they use all manner of strategies to part victims with their cash. BioCatch’s research shows that 90% of all scams take place via a mobile phone, with romance scams increasing by 23% on the last year and investment scams the most costly, with an average case value of $6,600.
BioCatch has identified that artificial intelligence techniques are used by both the scammers and the banks.
"Social engineering scams have not suddenly become less prevalent or sophisticated," noted Director of Global Fraud Intelligence at BioCatch, Thomas Peacock. "If anything, artificial intelligence has lowered the barrier to entry for aspiring scammers, allowing more bad actors to create more convincing scams at a scale we’ve never seen before. In response, many banks have realised behavioural intelligence enables them to recognise signs of manipulation and coercion before an accountholder ever authorises a transaction.”
Theft without the break-in
The risk from banking scams relies on two key factors: the fraudsters’ use of manipulative, persuasive strategies to force an irrational financial-based panic in the victim, and the ease with which money can be moved around via a mobile banking app.
Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!
Although mobile banking is hugely convenient for honest citizens, it is also proving to be a boon for the scammers. As BioCatch’s Director of Global Advisory Jonathan Frost says, “Scammers don't need to break into an account if they can persuade the customer to move the money for them. That is the challenge banks face today with investment and romance scams, where customers are manipulated into making payments they believe are legitimate.”
Different territories have their own rules for helping victims of these scams. In the UK, protection is available. “Reimbursement in the UK protects victims financially after the event, but it does not stop the scam from succeeding. The priority now has to be preventing the payment from reaching the criminal in the first place.”
The challenge is to ensure everyone knows the risks from banking scams.

articles.title: Fini le robot coincé sous les chaises : SwitchBot dégaine un mini-aspirateur surpuissant
articles.text:
Fini le robot coincé sous les chaises : SwitchBot dégaine un mini-aspirateur surpuissant
Le ménage au petit format
Avec ses 24,8 cm de diamètre, le SwitchBot K11+ Pro mise sur un format compact pour circuler entre les meubles. Cet aspirateur robot à 399,99 € offre une puissance de 12 000 Pa, deux brosses anti-emmêlement et une station de vidage automatique.
SwitchBot K11+ Pro
Même si les aspirateurs robots ne manquent pas de puissance sur leur fiche technique, encore faut-il qu'ils puissent passer entre les pieds d'une chaise. C'est sur ce terrain que SwitchBot positionne son K11+ Pro : un modèle destiné aux appartements, aux petits logements et aux pièces densément meublées. Le fabricant conserve un gabarit réduit tout en annonçant une aspiration renforcée et plusieurs dispositifs pour limiter l'entretien.
Le K11+ Pro mesure en effet 24,8 cm de diamètre pour 9,2 cm de hauteur. Son format doit faciliter les passages entre les pieds des meubles et sous ceux qui offrent suffisamment de dégagement.
Pour se repérer, le robot associe un LiDAR chargé de la cartographie à des capteurs de proximité destinés à détecter les pieds de meubles et les bords des murs. Il peut mémoriser jusqu'à cinq cartes, ce qui permet d'organiser le nettoyage sur plusieurs étages. Son poids d'environ 2,3 kg devrait aussi faciliter le transport de l'un à l'autre.
SwitchBot annonce une puissance maximale de 12 000 Pa, soit le double de celle du K11+ et quatre fois celle du K10+ Pro que nous avions testé. Une brosse principale entièrement en caoutchouc et une brosse latérale à deux bras sont conçues pour limiter l'enroulement des cheveux et des poils. La station vide automatiquement le bac du robot.
Le fabricant indique également un niveau sonore d'environ 45 dB en mode silencieux. Des lingettes jetables complètent l'équipement pour un nettoyage à sec. Disponible en noir et en blanc, le SwitchBot K11+ Pro est annoncé au prix conseillé de 399,99 €, sur le site de la marque et sur Amazon. Notez qu'une remise de 40% est proposée sur Amazon jusqu'au 5 octobre, soit un prix final de 239,99 €.
