articles.title: Saros 20 Flow Complete : Roborock change sa façon de laver les sols avec ce robot à rouleau — Frandroid
articles.text:
Faire le ménage au quotidien est devenu une routine facile. Vous lancez votre robot laveur et le sol devient propre en l’espace de quelques minutes. Mais certaines taches récalcitrantes demandent un soin particulier que les serpillières rotatives ne peuvent pas apporter.
Pour régler ce problème, Roborock a présenté début septembre, au salon IFA de Berlin, le Saros 20 Flow Complete. Il rejoint la nouvelle gamme comprenant le Saros 20 et le Saros 20 Sonic et apporte un tout nouveau système de lavage. À la manière des aspirateurs balais laveurs, il utilise un rouleau nettoyant à la place des serpillières plates habituelles.
Lancé à 1 299 euros, le nouveau Roborock Saros 20 Flow Complete fait entrer la serpillière à rouleau dans la gamme Saros, le haut de gamme de Roborock.
Une serpillière à rouleau pour s’attaquer aux taches en continu
La grosse innovation du Saros 20 Flow Complete ne se voit pas au premier coup d’œil, puisqu’elle se trouve sous le robot. Roborock mise en effet sur un nouveau système de lavage baptisé SpiraFlow 2.0, avec une serpillière à rouleau qui tourne en continu.
Le rouleau atteint 240 tours par minute et exerce une pression de 15 N sur le sol. Pendant qu’il tourne, 16 buses sous pression l’alimentent en permanence en eau propre. Dans le même temps, un racloir retire l’eau sale et les saletés récupérées, avant de les envoyer vers un réservoir séparé. Le rouleau reste ainsi propre durant tout le nettoyage, ce qui permet de laver le sol en un seul passage.
Le nettoyage des bordures a également été revu. Le robot embarque des brosses latérales à double arc relevables, et Roborock annonce une couverture de balayage des bords de 100 %. De quoi mieux récupérer poussières et petits débris le long des plinthes, là où les robots aspirateurs peinent souvent.
Une fois le ménage terminé, le robot retourne sur sa station RockDock, qui s’occupe de l’entretien. Le rouleau y est lavé à l’eau chaude jusqu’à 100 °C, puis séché à l’air chaud à 63 °C. Il est ainsi prêt pour le nettoyage suivant, sans que vous ayez à y toucher.
La puissance pour ne rien laisser traîner
Au-delà du lavage, le Saros 20 Flow Complete gère aussi les poussières, les poils et les petits débris, avec une puissance d’aspiration annoncée jusqu’à 36 000 Pa. Un niveau pensé pour les logements dont les sols alternent entre parquet, carrelage, tapis ou moquette.
Pour naviguer correctement dans ces espaces, le robot s’appuie sur le système RetractSense LiDAR pour cartographier les pièces et se repérer pendant ses déplacements. À cela s’ajoute Reactive AI, chargé d’identifier les objets laissés au sol : Roborock annonce une reconnaissance de plus de 300 types d’obstacles, aussi bien dans une pièce éclairée que dans l’obscurité.
Le Saros 20 Flow Complete se glisse partout
Avec seulement 8,98 cm de haut, le Saros 20 Flow Complete peut passer sous une grande majorité de meubles, du lit à l’armoire de grand-mère. Roborock le présente d’ailleurs comme le robot aspirateur à rouleau le plus fin du marché.
Son système AdaptiLift Traverse 3.0 lui permet aussi de franchir des seuils à double niveau allant jusqu’à 8,8 cmde haut. Il peut passer plus facilement d’une pièce à l’autre, même avec des barres de seuil marquées ou des différences de hauteur importantes. Plus besoin de le porter jusqu’à sa prochaine zone de nettoyage.
Si votre logement compte de nombreux tapis ou mélange carrelage, lino et parquet, le Saros 20 Flow Complete adapte sa hauteur au sol pour assurer un nettoyage optimal.
Le Roborock Saros 20 Flow Complete est disponible en noir ou en blanc, à 1 299 euros, sur le site du constructeur ou sur sa boutique officielle Amazon.

articles.title: The Best 1440p QD-OLED Monitors for Less Than $500
articles.text:
Today we're taking a comprehensive look at budget 1440p QD-OLED gaming monitors. This category offers fantastic value at the moment, with plenty of options available below $500. In fact, over the last couple of months we've seen some models drop as low as $300, which is pretty crazy.
For this round-up, we've tested 11 different monitors, including quite a few models we haven't covered before. The goal is to compare the options that matter most and hopefully make it easier to narrow down your buying decision.
Before getting into each monitor, there's one important detail you need to know. When shopping for a 27-inch 1440p QD-OLED, you'll generally encounter three different panel variants, often within a similar price range and sometimes separated by less than $100. All use the same generation of QD-OLED technology, so the fundamental hardware is largely similar across the range. However, the three variants are:
- 1440p, 280Hz, with full brightness capabilities
- 1440p, 240Hz, with full brightness capabilities
- 1440p, 240Hz, with limited brightness capabilities
There's an obvious trap here. Two of these panels run at 240Hz, but one can reach up to 1,000 nits of peak brightness, while the other is limited to just 400 nits.
That's a problem because when you see a 1440p 240Hz QD-OLED listed at a retailer, it isn't immediately obvious which version you're getting. Things become even more confusing when both options are priced similarly. Some brands are also being a little deceptive here, in our view, using very similar names for the full- and limited-brightness variants. That only adds to the confusion when browsing through the available models.
Making matters worse, the limited-brightness panel arrived well after the full-brightness version. QD-OLED established itself as a monitor technology capable of around 1,000 nits of peak brightness, and for a while that was what buyers could expect from essentially every model. Then, somewhat quietly, this nerfed 400-nit panel began appearing on the market.
Throughout this round-up we'll make it clear which monitor uses which panel, but there are also a few ways you can double-check this yourself. One option is our website, Monitor Deals. We've validated the specifications for every product included on the site and clearly identify which panel each monitor uses. Product pages also include a warning when a model has lower brightness than you might expect, while our similar-monitors feature groups together products that use identical panels.
You can also look closely at the manufacturer's spec sheet. The 280Hz panel is always the full-brightness variant. For 240Hz models, full-brightness versions are typically rated for 250 nits of SDR brightness, 1,000 nits peak HDR brightness, and DisplayHDR 400 certification. The limited-brightness models lack DisplayHDR 400 certification and are rated for just 200 nits SDR and 400 nits HDR. If you see those specifications on a product page, you're probably looking at the limited-brightness panel.
A Quick Look at the Monitors
| Monitor | Refresh Rate | Brightness Tier | SDR / Peak HDR | Recent Pricing | 
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Dell Alienware AW2725D | 280Hz | Full | 250 / 1,000 nits | $400 | 
| MSI MAG 271QP X28 | 280Hz | Full | 250 / 1,000 nits | $450 | 
| MSI MAG 273QP X24 | 240Hz | Full | 250 / 1,000 nits | – | 
| MSI MAG 271QPX E2 | 240Hz | Full | 250 / 1,000 nits | $350 | 
| Gigabyte MO27Q2 | 240Hz | Full | 250 / 1,000 nits | <$600 | 
| Acer Predator X27U X1 | 240Hz | Full | 250 / 1,000 nits | $450 | 
| Dell Alienware AW2726DM | 240Hz | Limited | 200 / 400 nits | $350 | 
| Gigabyte GO27Q24A | 240Hz | Limited | 200 / 400 nits | $350 | 
| AOC Q27G40ZDF | 240Hz | Limited | 200 / 400 nits | – | 
| Asus ROG Strix XG27AQDMES | 240Hz | Limited | 200 / 400 nits | $400 | 
| MSI MAG 272QP X24 | 240Hz | Limited | 200 / 400 nits | $400 | 
Let's start with the 280Hz models.
The first is the Dell Alienware AW2725D, which we reviewed in 2025. It has an MSRP of $550, but has recently been discounted to $400, and we'd expect to see sales around that price regularly from here on.
The other 280Hz option in this round-up is the MSI MAG 271QP X28, which has an MSRP of $500 but is more typically found for around $450. Both the Dell and MSI models offer the full brightness capabilities of these 1440p QD-OLED panels, reaching up to 1,000 nits peak.
Next are the 240Hz models using full-brightness panels.
For some reason, MSI has produced multiple versions based on this panel, so we've included both the MAG 273QP X24 and the older MAG 271QPX E2. The E2 can occasionally be found for around $350, while the 273QP X24 has been discontinued in some markets. MSI's 271QP X24 is a minor variant of the 273QP X24 with a slightly different design, although we haven't tested that particular model.
The Gigabyte MO27Q2 is another 240Hz full-brightness option, which we reviewed in 2025. It launched at $600 but was frequently sold below that price, and it's still available in some regions despite largely being replaced by the MO27Q2A, which uses a 280Hz panel.
We've also tested the Acer Predator X27U X1, which is commonly found for around $400 to $450. Acer offers several X27U models: the X1 tested here uses the 240Hz full-brightness panel, the Z1 uses the 280Hz panel, and the W1 uses the lower-brightness 240Hz panel.
All three models look very similar, and Acer's naming scheme doesn't make them especially easy to distinguish. For this round-up, though, we're specifically testing the 240Hz X1.
The Lower-Brightness 240Hz Models
Then we get to the 240Hz models using the limited-brightness panel.
One we've already reviewed is the Dell Alienware AW2726DM, which made a huge splash when it launched with an MSRP of just $350. That aggressive price forced a number of other QD-OLED manufacturers to respond and helped push prices down across the category.
We also have the Gigabyte GO27Q24A, which carries an MSRP of $450 but typically sells for around $350, matching the Alienware. Gigabyte has actually done a decent job with its naming scheme here. A G at the beginning indicates the lower-cost, lower-spec variant, while an M indicates a step up with full-brightness capabilities. Just watch the letter at the end. The GO27Q24A is the QD-OLED model, while the GO27Q24G uses a WOLED panel.
The AOC Q27G40ZDF is another low-cost 240Hz QD-OLED, although AOC appears to offer several variants using this limited-brightness panel depending on the retailer and region.
Also in the same family are the Q27G41ZDF and Q27GAZD. All three are extremely similar, so our findings for the G40ZDF should broadly apply to the other two models. Even the design and connectivity are essentially the same.
The ROG Strix XG27AQDMES is Asus' take on the 240Hz limited-brightness panel. It bizarrely launched with an MSRP of $600, though more recently it has been available for around $400.
Lastly, we have the MSI MAG 272QP X24, which also uses the lower-brightness 240Hz panel.
This is where MSI's line-up becomes particularly confusing and, in our opinion, somewhat deceptive. The 272QP X24 and very similar 274QP X24 both use the limited-brightness panel and are typically available for $350 to $400. Meanwhile, the 271QP X24 and 273QP X24 both use the full-brightness 240Hz panel.
That's nowhere near enough differentiation in the naming. If anything, the model numbers make the limited-brightness versions sound newer or higher-end, with the 274QP appearing to sit above the 273QP. So if you're shopping for an MSI QD-OLED, you'll need to pay very close attention to the exact model number. A single digit in the middle of the product name can determine which panel you're actually getting.
These aren't all of the budget 1440p QD-OLEDs currently on the market. As mentioned, there are several minor variants of the products we're testing here, along with a handful of models we haven't been able to get our hands on yet. We'll continue to test more monitors in this category, but these 11 models provide a good starting point for understanding the current budget QD-OLED landscape.
QD-OLED Similarities: Panel Coating and Subpixel Layout
While there are three panel variants used across these budget QD-OLED monitors, all of them use the same generation of QD-OLED technology and share the same baseline capabilities. The panel structure, layout, per-pixel control, and deep-black performance are effectively identical across all 11 monitors in this round-up.
That means characteristics such as black depth, screen coating, and subpixel layout are the same regardless of which variant you buy.
The screen coating on all 11 models is the same glossy QD-OLED finish we've seen for several years now. Its main strengths are a grain-free appearance that delivers excellent clarity, along with very good reflection handling. Because it's glossy, there is still some mirror-like reflectivity, but direct reflections are generally more subdued than on many other glossy displays. If you're using the monitor in an environment where light sources aren't directly hitting the screen, it's a great coating that produces a vibrant, clear image.
The main weakness is ambient-light reflectivity. In moderately to brightly lit environments, QD-OLED panels reflect ambient light in a way that raises black levels and gives the screen a slight reddish-purple tint. Under these conditions, blacks can appear gray rather than properly black, reducing one of OLED's biggest advantages.
You can mitigate this by positioning light sources so they don't hit the display directly, but that won't be practical for everyone. Ultimately, it's a limitation of this type of panel, and one reason QD-OLED monitors are best suited to darker rooms where the strengths of the technology can really shine.
Text rendering is also identical across all of these budget 1440p QD-OLEDs because they use the same triangular RGB subpixel layout. Since this isn't a traditional RGB stripe, it isn't fully compatible with modern subpixel font-rendering techniques.
As a result, text quality isn't as good as on monitors that use a conventional RGB stripe, such as most LCDs. With the triangular RGB layout, you may notice faint pink and green fringing around the top and bottom edges of text, which reduces overall clarity and can be a downgrade if you're coming from an LCD.
Text Rendering Quality
That said, we've heard from plenty of users who barely notice the issue, so how distracting it is will depend on your sensitivity to these artifacts and how much time you spend reading text. The subpixel layout has essentially no impact when watching video or playing games, where these displays look excellent.
Brightness: SDR and HDR
Brightness is where the different panel variants start to separate more clearly, which makes sense given that some are designed with limited brightness while others offer the full capabilities of QD-OLED. This affects both SDR and HDR performance, starting with SDR.
All of the full-brightness monitors are capable of around 250 nits in full-screen white SDR content, with no meaningful difference between them. The limited-brightness models, meanwhile, typically achieve around 190 to 200 nits. There's slightly more variation within this lower-brightness group. For example, we measured the Gigabyte GO27Q24A at around 8% brighter than the Dell AW2726DM, but broadly speaking these are 200-nit displays.
That means the full-brightness models are ultimately capable of around 25% higher SDR brightness.
But does that actually matter? It depends on your use case.
We generally find 200 nits sufficient for indoor use in a moderately lit or darker room, particularly where glare isn't an issue. In those conditions, we'd often turn down a 250-nit monitor anyway for a more comfortable viewing experience.
But if you use your monitor in a brighter room, deal with significant glare, need extra brightness to overcome reflections, or simply prefer running your display at high brightness levels, 200 nits may not be enough. In that situation, opting for a full-brightness QD-OLED makes much more sense.
Minimum brightness is very good across the board. The highest minimum we measured was around 30 nits, which is already quite low and should be perfectly usable in dark environments. A few monitors can get much dimmer, particularly the Asus and AOC models, although we're not sure how practical it would be to actually use one at around 10 nits.
HDR Is Where the Gap Gets Much Larger
The difference between the limited- and full-brightness panels becomes much more pronounced in HDR. Starting again with full-screen brightness, performance is broadly similar to what we saw in SDR. The full-brightness models sit between roughly 250 and 270 nits, while the limited-brightness models range from around 186 to 216 nits. The AOC and Dell models post particularly low results here compared with the rest of the group.
The gap narrows somewhat with a 10% window, although the full-brightness models still hold an advantage. Most of them deliver between 455 and 485 nits, a spread of only around 7% from the lowest to highest result.
The limited-brightness models fall between roughly 380 and 435 nits. In the worst cases, that's up to 20% dimmer than the full-brightness models, although some get surprisingly close. The Gigabyte GO27Q24A, for example, trails the higher-tier models by only around 20 nits.
The biggest difference appears in peak brightness, represented by our 2% window test. All six full-brightness monitors we tested are capable of exceeding 1,000 nits. None of the limited-brightness models reaches even 450 nits.
That's a massive difference. In the best cases, the full-brightness models can deliver more than twice the peak luminance of the limited variants. Interestingly, even when the full-brightness models are switched into their "True Black" modes, which typically reduce peak brightness in exchange for improved accuracy, they still slightly outperform the limited-brightness models. So while the size of the advantage varies depending on the content and window size, the full-brightness models are consistently brighter.
For the written version of this round-up, we've deliberately skipped some of the deeper testing around HDR mode configurations, HDR and SDR calibration, and color accuracy to keep the article focused on the information most relevant to a buying decision. Those results are covered in detail in the video for readers who want to dig further into the data.
Ports and Features
Connectivity is fairly basic on most of these monitors. The AOC Q27G40ZDF has the weakest port selection, with just one DisplayPort input, one HDMI port limited to HDMI 2.0 speeds, and no USB ports at all. The Dell AW2726DM is also fairly lackluster, although it at least provides two HDMI 2.0 ports.
Every other model offers HDMI 2.1 alongside a DisplayPort 1.4 connection.
| Monitor | DisplayPort | HDMI | USB-C | USB Hub | USB Hub Speed | KVM Switch | Power Supply | 
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Acer Predator X27U X1 | 1x 1.4 DSC | 2x 2.1 48 Gbps | No | No | No | No | External Brick | 
| AOC Q27G40ZDF | 1x 1.4 DSC | 1x 2.0 18 Gbps | No | No | No | No | Internal | 
| Asus ROG Strix XG27AQDMES | 1x 1.4 DSC | 2x 2.1 48 Gbps | Yes (service only) | No | No | No | Internal | 
| Dell Alienware AW2725D | 1x 1.4 DSC | 2x 2.1 48 Gbps | Yes, 15W PD (no DP-Alt) | Yes, 2 Port | 5 Gbps | No | Internal | 
| Dell Alienware AW2726DM | 1x 1.4 DSC | 2x 2.0 18 Gbps | No | No | No | No | Internal | 
| Gigabyte GO27Q24A | 1x 1.4 DSC | 2x 2.1 48 Gbps | No | No | No | No | Internal | 
| Gigabyte MO27Q2 | 1x 1.4 DSC | 2x 2.1 48 Gbps | Yes, 18W PD, DP-Alt | Yes, 2 Port | 5 Gbps | Yes | Internal | 
| MSI MAG 271QP X28 | 1x 1.4 DSC | 2x 2.1 48 Gbps | Yes, 15W PD, DP-Alt | No | No | No | Internal | 
| MSI MAG 271QPX E2 | 1x 1.4 DSC | 2x 2.1 48 Gbps | Yes, 15W PD, DP-Alt | No | No | No | Internal | 
| MSI MAG 272QP X24 | 1x 1.4 DSC | 2x 2.1 40 Gbps | Yes, 15W PD, DP-Alt | No | No | No | Internal | 
| MSI MAG 273QP X24 | 1x 1.4 DSC | 2x 2.1 48 Gbps | No | No | No | No | External Brick | 
Several monitors also include USB-C, although the implementation varies. On the Dell AW2725D, USB-C does not function as a display input, while on the Asus XG27AQDMES it is reserved for service use.
Three of the MSI models support DisplayPort Alt Mode over USB-C with 15W of power delivery, although they don't include additional USB ports. Only two monitors offer a proper USB hub: the Dell AW2725D and Gigabyte MO27Q2. Of those, only the Gigabyte also includes KVM functionality and USB-C with DP Alt Mode.
From a connectivity standpoint, the MO27Q2 clearly has the strongest port selection of the group, although most of the other models still provide a basic but sufficient set of inputs.
Useful OSD Features
Each monitor includes additional features accessible through the OSD, and most provide the usual mix of color controls and gaming features such as crosshairs and FPS counters. Rather than going through every common setting, we'll focus on the more notable differences we found during testing.
The Asus XG27AQDMES is the only model here with a proximity sensor that can automatically switch off the OLED panel when you leave your desk. We've seen this feature implemented across several Asus OLED monitors, and we're pleased to see it make its way to the more affordable AQDMES as well. It works well and is a useful complement to the other OLED care features.
Several displays also include black frame insertion, which can operate at 120Hz to provide motion clarity closer to 240Hz. As we've mentioned in previous reviews, however, this is a fairly inflexible feature because it requires disabling variable refresh rate support. The monitors that include this are the MSI 271QP X28 and 272QP X24 (labeled MPRT), the Asus XG27AQDMES (labeled ELMB) and the Gigabyte GO27Q24A (labeled Ultra Clear).
Two models also include an Anti-Flicker feature: the Asus XG27AQDMES and Gigabyte GO27Q24A. This lets you raise the minimum refresh rate used during variable refresh operation, which can help reduce flicker when frame rates fluctuate heavily. It's a moderately useful feature and we're glad to see it included, even if it's not a game changer.
Acer's HDR Switching Is a Pain
On a more negative note, the Acer Predator X27U X1 handles switching between SDR and HDR very poorly. There is an "Auto" HDR mode, but it isn't actually automatic. Selecting this option keeps the monitor in its HDR configuration even when HDR is disabled in the operating system, which can lead to incorrect-looking colors.
For the best experience, you need to manually change OSD settings depending on whether you're using SDR or HDR, which is unnecessarily cumbersome. The monitor also has particularly annoying OLED panel-cleaning warnings compared with the other models. They appear frequently and require user interaction before disappearing.
OLED Care and Burn-In Warranties
Each display includes a different set of OLED care controls for features such as automatic dimming, edge dimming, pixel shifting, and related protections. Having some control over these features is useful, particularly if you find certain dimming behaviors distracting or overly aggressive.
MSI does the best job here, offering both the ability to disable some OLED care functions and adjust others, including the delay before dimming activates and the strength of the dimming effect. The AOC also provides some customization for individual OLED care features, although not to the same extent as the MSI models.
Asus offers a good range of options as well, though most are simple on/off toggles. Gigabyte's implementation is similar, but with slightly fewer controls. Acer provides only a handful of OLED care settings, while Dell offers no user control over these features at all, making its monitors the weakest in this area.
As for burn-in, all of these monitors use fundamentally similar panel hardware, so the underlying risk of permanent image retention should be broadly comparable. Actual behavior will still depend on usage patterns and which OLED care features are enabled, but at the hardware level these panels use the same type of emissive technology.
Based on publicly available warranty information, all six brands represented in this round-up offer a three-year burn-in warranty for these displays, which has effectively become the industry standard.
Monitor Design and Build Quality
We're not going to spend too much time on aesthetics because monitor design is ultimately subjective. You may simply prefer the look of one model over another, and that's perfectly reasonable. However, there are some meaningful differences in ergonomics, stand design, build quality, and general usability.
The AOC Q27G40ZDF, along with its closely related variants, uses a fixed-height stand. It's the only monitor in this round-up that doesn't offer height adjustment. That's a significant downside, especially because the AOC isn't substantially cheaper than many competing models that do provide a fully adjustable stand. Build quality is also fairly basic, and the monitor lacks a directional joystick for navigating the OSD. Instead, menu navigation is more cumbersome than it needs to be.
Every other monitor here includes a directional control, so from an ergonomic and usability perspective, the AOC is the weakest of the group.
The Dell AW2726DM is also relatively basic, although it does include height adjustment.
MSI's models are broadly similar to one another in both styling and build quality. They're perfectly acceptable overall, without doing anything particularly noteworthy.
The Acer Predator X27U X1 uses a wide V-shaped stand base. Personally, we don't think this works as well as the smaller, flatter bases used by many of the competing models because it occupies noticeably more desk space.
Gigabyte's design is one of our favorites in this group, and it's used across both the M-series and G-series models with only minor variations. You get a height-adjustable stand, a directional joystick for the OSD, and a very nice metal stand base with a thin metal pillar. Build quality is excellent for a budget-oriented product.
The Asus XG27AQDMES is also particularly well built, with a compact metal stand base and above-average overall construction. Lastly, the Dell AW2725D is another strong design. Although most of its external surfaces are plastic, the quality and finish of that plastic are noticeably better than on many of the other monitors in this round-up.
Picking Winners: The Best Options
As we've emphasized throughout this article, the most important thing to understand is that there are two versions of the 240Hz 1440p QD-OLED panel: one with the usual 1,000-nit peak brightness capability, and another limited to around 400 nits. It's not always obvious which panel a monitor is using, but this is one of the biggest differences between the options on the market today.
The 1,000-nit panel is simply better. Everything the limited-brightness 400-nit panel can do, the full-brightness version can also do, while adding around 25% higher SDR brightness and a huge increase in peak HDR output. In our view, the full-brightness panel is also the only one of the two that delivers a genuinely convincing HDR experience. So if two monitors cost roughly the same and one uses the full-brightness panel while the other doesn't, the choice is obvious.
How Much Should You Pay?
The going rate for a 27-inch 1440p limited-brightness QD-OLED is around $350. Multiple models are regularly available at that price, and we wouldn't pay more than $350 for this panel regardless of the official MSRP. Closer to $300 is even better, and we've seen some models approach that level over the last few months.
Given the HDR performance advantage, we'd be comfortable paying around 25% more for a full-brightness model. Around $400 is an excellent deal, while $450 is still reasonable.
The good news is that most of the monitors covered here have already been available within those price ranges. The 280Hz Alienware AW2725D, for example, recently dropped to $400. The MSI 271QP X28 is regularly available for around $450, while most of the 240Hz limited-brightness models sell for $350 or less.
The Best Budget QD-OLED Options
It's encouraging that most of these 1440p QD-OLED monitors are genuinely good. There isn't a single model in this round-up that we'd avoid entirely because of a major flaw. Regional pricing also varies significantly, so any of them could make sense if heavily discounted.
If you're on a tighter budget and simply want the cheapest good-value QD-OLED, this is where the limited-brightness models make the most sense. They still provide a high refresh rate, excellent motion clarity, very good image quality, and the outstanding contrast you'd expect from OLED.
We tested five models in this category and ended up with two clear standouts. The Gigabyte GO27Q24A is our preferred option, with better HDR and SDR calibration, a higher-quality design, and a stronger feature set than the rest of the group. The MSI 272QP X24 is a close second and also a strong choice at the right price.
Our Top Overall Pick: Dell Alienware AW2725D
The Dell Alienware AW2725D is our top overall pick. It delivers well-balanced performance across both SDR and HDR, generally strong calibration, a higher 280Hz refresh rate, and a very good physical design. There are a few weaknesses. Dell provides no customization for its OLED care features, and the monitor lacks a boosted-brightness HDR mode. But across the complete package, we think the AW2725D strikes the best balance of the models tested here.
At its original $550 MSRP, it isn't especially compelling today. At around $400 on sale, however, it becomes a much stronger proposition. We've already seen it reach that price, and with the holiday shopping period approaching, we'd expect similar discounts to appear again.
As for the other full-brightness options, the Acer Predator X27U X1 loses points because of its awkward SDR-to-HDR switching. The Gigabyte MO27Q2 lacks a proper "Peak" HDR mode and is becoming difficult to find, having largely been replaced by the newer MO27Q2A.
The MSI 271QPX E2 has the weakest calibration among the full-brightness models and doesn't offer enough standout features to compensate. We also weren't overly impressed with the MSI 271QP X28. Its 280Hz refresh rate is a plus, but it suffers from noticeable black crush in SDR, although HDR performance is better and it supports all three major HDR configurations.
The MSI model we prefer is actually the 273QP X24, but it has some HDR saturation issues and has been discontinued in several markets, making it difficult to recommend broadly.

articles.title: The rise, fall, and rise of portable MP3 players
articles.text:
This is The Stepback, a weekly newsletter breaking down one essential story from the tech world. For more on the collapse and the resurgence of the portable media player, follow Terrence O’Brien. The Stepback arrives in our subscribers’ inboxes on Sunday at 8AM ET. Opt in for The Stepback here.
The rise, fall, and rise of portable MP3 players
Apple perfected the media player with the iPod, then abandoned it.
The rise, fall, and rise of portable MP3 players
Apple perfected the media player with the iPod, then abandoned it.
How it started
We are spoiled for choice, musically. Most of us walk around with access to hundreds of millions of songs in our pockets. But it wasn’t until 1998 that portable digital music was even a thing. Before that we lugged booklets full of CDs on the bus or stashed a handful of cassettes in our backpacks. With the advent of the MP3 player in the 2000s we were soon able to carry massive libraries of music everywhere we went — over 1,000 albums’ worth depending on the file format and the size of your MP3 player.
The MPMan F10 is generally considered to be the first commercial MP3 player. It was roughly the size of a deck of cards and looked like an oversized pager. It launched in Asia in March of 1998, but it barely made a blip on anyone’s radar. It was the Diamond Rio PMP300 that broke through in the West a few months later, in September of 1998. It was slightly larger, and its design more closely resembles what we envision when we think of a media player (namely the iPod). But even then, it drew more attention because the Recording Industry Association of America (RIAA) sued Diamond Multimedia in an attempt to stop the spread of MP3s.
The F10 and the PMP300 were, unsurprisingly, primitive by today’s standards, shipping with just 32MB — yes, that’s megabytes — of storage. That tiny amount of built-in memory only allowed for around 12 songs to be stored on them. They held less audio than a CD and generally sounded worse. But it wasn’t that big of a limitation, in comparison to the nightmare that was the UI on their tiny monochrome LCDs. Plus, you could expand storage on both using SmartMedia cards if you really needed to.
Eventually, some companies addressed the storage issue by swapping flash storage, which was still relatively limited at the time, for traditional spinning-disc hard drives. The Creative Nomad Jukebox, for instance, had a 6GB drive inside. It also had a more familiar design modeled after portable CD players. But that made it bulkier than the competition; it weighed a shocking 14 ounces. Unsurprisingly, it also failed to usher MP3 players into the mainstream.
It wasn’t until the introduction of the iPod in November 2001 that the golden age of portable media players truly took off. By 2007, roughly 20 percent of Americans owned a personal media player. Other companies, including Microsoft and Creative, tried to carve out space for themselves with Zune and Zen lines, respectively. But Apple’s iPod was the dominant force in the market, accounting for over 70 percent of media player sales.
While 20 percent isn’t ubiquitous, the iPod and the digital music revolution certainly felt inescapable in the 2000s. Bands like Radiohead and Nine Inch Nails were experimenting with pay-what-you-want digital releases. Napster taught everyone the phrases “file sharing” and “peer-to-peer.” And Apple’s iconic ads combining silhouettes and white earbuds were everywhere.
The personal media player’s spotlight was relatively short-lived. While Apple didn’t fully discontinue the iPod lineup until 2022, it retired the Classic model in 2014 and cut the Nano and Shuffle in 2017, leaving the iPod Touch — essentially an iPhone without the phone — as the last iPod standing.
By 2011, the writing was on the wall as iPhone sales eclipsed iPod sales for the first time. The portable media player market shrank quickly as modern smartphones replaced flip phones and BlackBerrys, and music consumption moved away from purchasing CDs or digital downloads toward streaming. What was, at its peak, a $21.6 billion industry in 2008 had collapsed to just $613 million in 2012, according to research firm Mintel.
How it’s going
It’s difficult to get reliable numbers for the size of the digital audio player market these days. Some research firms lump all media players together, regardless of whether they’re audio or video, streaming or offline. Others that do track audio-specific players as a separate market segment can’t seem to agree. Some report that it’s a $180 million-plus industry on the rise. Others say it’s only a $1.2 million market and it’s shrinking. One thing is certain, though: Portable media players have become a very small niche.
For most of the last 10 years, dedicated portable music players were primarily the realm of audiophiles. Companies like Sony and Astell & Kern have been steadily releasing high-end audio players that can sell for well north of $3,000. Sony’s NW-A306 is the only device offered by either company that even approaches a mainstream consumer price, at $399.99.
These devices aren’t just more expensive, they’re more complicated than the iPods of yore. Wi-Fi and Bluetooth are a given. They feature large touchscreens and high-end digital audio converters. They also often run Android, opening them up to streaming apps like Spotify and Qobuz. Sony has fully embraced the iPod Touch model, giving its players full access to the Google Play store.
The sky-high prices and embrace of apps has led many to reject these players. Instead, those looking for an offline listening experience free from notifications and algorithms have turned to the past. Vintage iPods still fetch hundreds of dollars on eBay. An entire cottage industry has cropped up around modding them — adding modern features like Bluetooth and USB-C, replacing the dying hard drives and batteries, or just customizing the appearance.
What happens next
As popular as the iPod was, the world’s supply of working used units will eventually run out. As they age, batteries will stop holding a charge and spinning drives will fail, and most people don’t want to open up a piece of delicate electronics or mess with a soldering iron. But the renewed interest in iPods is starting to drive up prices on other media players, and modders are now swapping new drives into Zunes and selling them for hundred of dollars on eBay.
With Google searches for “MP3 player” nearly tripling since last year and The New York Times running trend pieces about the iPod resurgence, a number of companies and startups are trying to cash in. Chinese manufacturers have flooded AliExpress, Temu, and Amazon with a ton of dirt-cheap players and shameless iPod knockoffs.
Wildly successful crowdfunding campaigns, like that of the AP30 Music Boy, show there is pent-up demand for retro portable music players. But most out there aren’t moving the needle much in terms of design or usability.
Sleevenote is one startup that’s attempting to break the mold, but its success is far from guaranteed. It’s a startup from musician Tom Vek that embraces some modern conveniences like syncing over Wi-Fi and Bluetooth headphones, but skips on any extraneous features like streaming, apps, or games. It swaps scrolling text lists of artist names for a grid of album art. It’s highly visual, and attempts to re-create the experience of paging through a CD booklet. It also has limited integration with a host of digital music storefronts like Bandcamp, Subvert, Bleep, Qobuz, Amazon Music, and more.
Vek has a promising-looking concept on its hands that actually approaches the portable media player in a fresh way. But the bulky Day One edition still has a lot of kinks to work out, including disappointing battery life. (I’ve been testing one for a couple of months now.) Plus, it’s currently sold out and the company doesn’t know when the next batch will be made available.
There’s growing anti-streaming sentiment, and the slowtech trend doesn’t seem to be going anywhere anytime soon. But no obvious heir to the iPod throne has stepped in to fill the gap in the MP3 player market.
It seems unlikely that the MP3 player will see a resurgence on the scale of vinyl or even CDs. In part because, for whatever convenience advantage an iPod might have over a limited edition LP, it lacks the collectibility factor. And that has been a major driver of the physical media resurgence, as evidenced by the fact that, while Gen Z and millennials might be buying up CDs in record numbers, half of them don’t own a CD player.
By the way
- Suzanne Vega is sometimes called the “mother of the MP3.” Karlheinz Brandenburg was working on audio compression technology at the Fraunhofer Society (FHG) in Germany and turned to Vega’s “Tom’s Diner” as his benchmark due to her “warm, human voice” that would be a challenge to encode. Thousands of miles away, James Johnston also turned to “Tom’s Diner” while working on audio compression at Bell Labs. Brandenburg and Johnston’s work ultimately led to the creation of MPEG-1 Audio Layer III standard, better known as MP3.
- Kane Kramer is widely credited with inventing the first digital audio player in 1979, and successfully patented it in the UK in 1985, and the US in 1987. Many of its features, including an online music store, would eventually find their way into the iPod and iTunes. And Paul McCartney was an early financial backer, but his IXI never saw a commercial release. Kramer’s patents lapsed in 1988. While Apple eventually gave him credit for his invention, it was primarily a legal maneuver to undermine a company called Burst.com that sued Apple for patent infringement.
Read this
- Brandon Shaw, host of YouTube channel Digging the Greats, ditched streaming for an iPod two years ago and documented the experience over the course of several videos.
- The New York Times looked at how younger generations were embracing old-school media formats, including the iPod, in an attempt to break free of the shackles of streaming.
- The Verge crew shared their fond memories of the iPod when Apple officially put it out to pasture in 2022.
- This visual history of the iPod charts its evolution from clunky brick to sleek icon of modern design.

articles.title: LG OLED65B6 : cet excellent TV 4K (144 Hz) de 65 pouces perd déjà 400 € de son prix — Frandroid
articles.text:
Pas besoin de grimper jusqu’aux séries OLED evo pour profiter de la qualité d’image signée LG. Positionné juste en dessous des modèles C6 et G6 dans le catalogue 2026, le LG B6 est la porte d’entrée parfaite pour qui cherche un grand écran d’exception. Il reprend les fondamentaux de la marque : un contraste infini grâce aux noirs profonds, le traitement Dolby Vision et des fonctionnalités gaming dernier cri pour vos consoles. En ce moment, la version 65 pouces s’affiche déjà avec 400 euros de réduction.
Les forces du LG OLED65B6
- Sa dalle OLED 4K de 65 pouces compatible Dolby Vision
- Quatre ports HDMI 4K 120 Hz compatibles G-Sync et FreeSync Premium
- Le processeur Alpha 8 AI 4K Gen3 et l’interface webOS 26
Sur le site officiel de LG, le téléviseur LG OLED65B6 peut vous revenir à 1 599 euros grâce à une ODR de 200 euros contre 1 999 euros de base.
Si, par la suite, l’offre mentionnée dans cet article n’est plus disponible, merci de jeter un coup d’œil ci-dessous afin de dénicher d’autres offres concernant le LG OLED65B6. Le tableau s’actualise automatiquement.
Une dalle OLED 4K pour les soirées cinéma
LG a particulièrement soigné la finition pour faire de sa série B6 un objet aussi discret qu’élégant. Grâce à un châssis fin et des bordures quasi invisibles, la TV se fond sans effort dans le décor de votre pièce. Résultat : pas de fioritures ni de cadres encombrants, seule l’immense image de 65 pouces prend toute la place pour vous plonger au cœur de vos films et jeux préférés.
Il utilise une dalle OLED moins lumineuse que ses homologues plus coûteux de la série C6, qui profite d’une dalle OLED Evo. Difficile de lui en tenir rigueur, quand elle profite des avantages de l’OLED, à savoir des noirs profonds, un contraste impressionnant et des couleurs vives.
Le traitement est confié au processeur Alpha 8 AI 4K Gen3, chargé de l’upscaling des sources en définition inférieure et du Dynamic Tone Mapping Pro. En HDR, le téléviseur prend en charge le Dolby Vision, le HDR10 et le HLG. Il propose aussi le Filmmaker Mode pour respecter l’image voulue par le réalisateur. Le HDR10+ n’est pas de la partie. Quant à l’audio, le son se limite à 20 W en 2.0 : une barre de son sera la bienvenue pour profiter du Dolby Atmos.
Un TV qui ne laisse pas les joueurs de côté
Les joueurs et joueuses y trouveront aussi leur compte avec ce téléviseur. Vous allez pouvoir enchaîner les parties sur PS5 ou Xbox Series X avec une grande fluidité en 4K@120 Hz grâce à ses ports HDMI 2.1 (ou 144 Hz en FHD). Il prend également en charge le VRR, ou taux de rafraîchissement variable, ainsi que l’ALLM, parfait pour combattre le phénomène de tearing, ou déchirure d’écran.
Terminons sur l’interface où l’on retrouve webOS 26 aux commandes. Une interface fluide et intuitive à utiliser. Bien entendu, on peut accéder rapidement aux applications phares, comme Netflix, Disney+, Prime Video ou YouTube et d’autres téléchargeables. Et ce modèle profite du programme Re:New, qui promet 4 mises à jour du système sur 5 ans.
Si vous souhaitez comparer ce B6 avec d’autres modèles plus abordables, jetez un œil à notre sélection des meilleures TV pas chères.

articles.title: Intel Xeon 6+ SKU List and Value Analysis: Clearwater Forest Runs Wide
articles.text:
Intel has been shipping its Xeon 6+ “Clearwater Forest” CPUs for just over a quarter now. The first server chips based on Intel’s 18A process node, the Clearwater Forest launch, have been a critical processor bring-up for the company. Not only does the Xeon 6+ chip family help Intel better address the market for high-core-count x86 CPUs, but it also helps fine-tune Intel’s fabs and Foveros Direct 3D packaging lines for what will be the real big test for Intel 18A(-P) server parts: 2027’s Diamond Rapids.
As part of this process, Intel has been ramping up Xeon 6+ chip production as part of the pipe-cleaning process. That means Xeon 6+ chips are finally becoming available to vendors outside the hyperscalers, who often have a quarter-plus lead on chip supply.
That leaves Intel customers with a simple but important question: which Xeon 6+ chip SKUs should they go with? Clearwater Falls has a rather short product stack, with just 4 physical SKUs. That still leaves several important factors to weigh across different metrics, including total performance, TDPs, and core-to-memory (and core-to-cache) ratios. So here is ServeTheHome’s look at the Xeon 6+ product stack, and what some of the best options are for different scenarios/optimization points.
Intel Xeon 6+ Chip SKUs: 144 to 288 Cores, $5K to $15K
First up, here is the complete list of Xeon 6+ chip SKUs.
The good news is that Intel is not gating any features behind specific SKUs, which has historically been a chip-differentiation technique they have used heavily in server processors. With the Xeon E-core lineup far more focused on high-core-count use cases than anything else, Intel is not withholding any features from any SKUs. That means customers get it all: 2 socket support, 12 channels of DDR5 (and MRDIMM) memory, 96 PCIe lanes, and Intel’s new Application Energy Telemetry (AET) for per-application core energy reporting.
Consequently, the only real decisions are core counts, power consumption, and all the second-order effects.
On the power consumption front in particular, Intel’s Speed Select Technology (SST-PP) adds an extra wrinkle: it lets select SKUs run at one of two TDPs. Specifically, both the top-tier 6990E+ and second-tier 6980E+ support this feature. Higher TDP modes allow for higher guaranteed base clocks and higher all-core turbo clocks, while lower TDPs keep the chips running cooler and closer to their ideal point on the power/frequency curve.
For a true “all performance at any cost” scenario, the 288-core Intel Xeon 6990E+ in high-TDP mode is the big winner. With 288 cores at an average all-core turbo speed of 2.8GHz, it offers the highest total throughput. The trade-off is that it is also the most power-hungry option at a chip level, with a TDP of 450 Watts.
Alternatively, the chip can run in low-TDP mode, which drops all-core turbo speeds by 14% to 2.4GHz, while the TDP drops by 27% (120W) to 330W. Coincidentally, this also matches the top TDP of Intel’s previous-generation Xeon 6E (Sierra Forest) chips, though those are Xeon 6780E parts with fewer memory channels in a smaller socket.
With all TDPs at 300 Watts or higher, this means the high-core-count chips in their low-TDP modes offer the best overall efficiency on a watts-per-core basis. The low-TDP 6990E+ is just 1.15W/core, and the 6980E+ in low-TDP mode slides in right under that at 1.14W/core. For some sense, a 192-core AMD EPYC 9965 ranges between 2.34W/core and 2.60W/core. AMD’s core is a P-core not an E-core with its same Zen 5 instruction set and two threads per. So if you were counting threads/ vCPUs, Intel’s parts are in a similar ballpark.
The advantage of going with smaller core count chips, in turn, is that the more energy-efficient chips have higher average clock speeds, especially at lower TDPs. By the time we get to the 144-core 6960E+, this chip will guarantee a base clock speed of 2.4GHz with an all-core turbo of 3.0GHz at 330 Watts, several hundred MHz (~25%) better than the 6990E+ at the same clock speed. Consequently, for workloads that need many cores but cannot scale to 288 cores, this is a sweet spot for the highest per-core performance in the Xeon 6+ family.
The smallest SKU is also the best point for L3 cache per core. While the amount of L3 cache scales down with core count (with Intel using salvaged base dies here), it does not scale down on a 1-to-1 basis with core count. As a result, while the 6990E+ has 2MB of L3 per core, that rises to 2.5MB per core for the 6970E+, and finally 3MB per core on the 6960E+.
Meanwhile, the relationship between cores and bandwidth is even greater as you go down the stack. As noted earlier, all chip SKUs get the same memory support. So, assuming 12 channels of DDR5-8000 MRDIMMs, this spans from 2.67GB/second of memory bandwidth per core for the 288-core SKU to 5.34GB/second for the 144-core SKU.
Finally, how does all of this look with pricing in mind? With the caveat that Intel’s list prices for server CPUs are traditionally discounted, this is how many cores $1000 buys you:
That means there is a very solid progression in both total cost and cost-per-core as you move up Intel’s Xeon 6+ SKU stack.
As you would expect, the 144-core Xeon 6960E+ is the cheapest chip, at a list price of just over $4600. That is followed by the 6970E+ at around $7700, the 6980E+ at $9900, and finally the flagship Xeon 6990E+ at just shy of $15,000. The number of cores you get per $1000 decreases much faster than the core counts increase. By the time you reach the Xeon 6990E+, that is around a 63% premium on per-core costs. Though a 144-core Xeon 6960E+ will not come anywhere close to the flagship Xeon 6990E+ chip’s total throughput in throughput-bound scenarios, the higher-cost chips still serve an important role in servers.
Final Words
Intel has kept the SKU stack for the Xeon 6+ family relatively simple for a server chip. That also makes decision-making easier for Intel’s customers.
The Xeon 6990E+ is bar none the fastest chip in the series in terms of total (on paper) compute throughput, thanks to its 288 cores. It is also the least cost-effective chip on a cost-per-core basis. Of course, the chip is just one part of the equation since memory costs often dominate server pricing these days. The smaller-core-count chips cannot push the same total throughput, but they can have more cache and memory bandwidth per core, plus slightly higher clock speeds. Thanks to Intel’s low-TDP SST-PP modes, the high-core-count chips are technically the most energy efficient on a per-core basis.
This underscores the importance of understanding the workload that will run on a Xeon 6+ server. Even with just 4 SKUs, the wide range in core counts (and fixed aspects elsewhere) means optimizing for compute, memory, and cost all have different optimal points. For Intel, that means the Xeon 6+ lineup can serve a wide range of customers, but customers need to do their homework to figure out what they need.

articles.title: Trump Names National Intelligence Director Jay Clayton to Lead a New Federal AI Task Force
articles.text:
President Donald Trump on Sunday tapped Jay Clayton, his director of national intelligence, to lead a new government task force on artificial intelligence.
Trump is calling it the “Super Intelligence Force,” because he has tried to rebrand AI as “super intelligence.” The announcement comes after Trump hosted top executives of AI companies at the White House last week and said they had signed a voluntary accord that would effectively self-police the development of the technology.
The task force will coordinate the federal effort “to ensure that America continues to lead the World in Super Intelligence, which many say is bigger than the Industrial Revolution, and the Internet, and will protect the interests, and improve the lives, of all Americans,” Trump in a post on social media Sunday.
The task force will reach out to consumers, public interest groups, religious organizations, critical infrastructure providers and AI companies, the Republican president said.
Others on the task force include the Federal Trade Commission’s chairman, Andrew Ferguson; Emil Michael, the Pentagon’s chief technology officer; and Scott Kupor, the director of the Office of Personnel Management.
The group will report to Trump and his chief of staff, Susie Wiles.
Related: Nvidia Unveils AI Agent Safety Platform With Hardware-Based Watchdog

Related: Autonomous AI Hacks Raise Thorny Questions of Legal Accountability

articles.title: Trump anuncia “força de superinteligência” para coordenar avanço da IA nos EUA
articles.text:
O presidente dos Estados Unidos, Donald Trump, anunciou, neste domingo (4), a criação da Super Intelligence Force (SIF) (Força da Superinteligência, na tradução literal), força-tarefa voltada à coordenação das ações do governo estaduniense relacionadas ao desenvolvimento da inteligência artificial (IA).
O anúncio ocorreu após Trump se reunir, na semana passada, com líderes das maiores empresas de IA dos Estados Unidos, em meio à crescente pressão pela criação de mecanismos de segurança para a tecnologia.
“Após o Histórico Acordo da Casa Branca sobre Superinteligência, no qual as empresas de tecnologia mais importantes do mundo se reuniram e confirmaram suas responsabilidades perante o povo americano, estou anunciando a formação da Super Intelligence Force (SIF)”, escreveu Trump em publicação no Truth Social.
Segundo o presidente, a força-tarefa vai coordenar ações com o governo federal para “garantir que a América continue liderando o mundo em superinteligência”.
O termo “superinteligência” passou a ser a expressão que Trump determinou que o governo federal utilize no lugar de “inteligência artificial”.
Quem vai comandar a força-tarefa
- Trump afirmou que a SIF será responsável por manter contato com consumidores, grupos de interesse público, organizações religiosas, fornecedores de infraestrutura e líderes do setor de tecnologia;
- O grupo será liderado pelo diretor de Inteligência Nacional dos Estados Unidos, Jay Clayton, que também deverá ocupar a posição de czar de IA;
- Além de Clayton, Trump anunciou que Andrew Ferguson, presidente da Comissão Federal de Comércio (FTC); Emil Michael, subsecretário de pesquisa e engenharia e diretor de tecnologia do Pentágono; e Scott Kupor, diretor do Escritório de Gestão de Pessoas, também estarão à frente da força-tarefa;
- Os quatro responderão diretamente a Trump e à chefe de gabinete da Casa Branca, Susie Wiles.
Leia mais:
- Trump janta com CEO da Anthropic em meio a tensões com a empresa e discussões sobre o futuro da IA
- Trump descarta criar regras para IA em parceria com a China
- IA terá quatro níveis de supervisão após acordo entre gigantes da tecnologia nos EUA
Empresas assumiram compromissos de segurança
O anúncio acontece poucos dias depois de Trump se reunir na Casa Branca com representantes de algumas das principais empresas de IA do país: OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Meta, Nvidia e SpaceXAI. Após o encontro, as empresas assinaram um conjunto de padrões voluntários de segurança para seus sistemas.
Trump classificou os compromissos como “moralmente vinculantes” e afirmou posteriormente que estava observando uma “tremenda autorregulação” por parte das companhias.
De acordo com uma cópia do acordo de uma página divulgada pelo presidente, as empresas se comprometeram a adotar quatro camadas de controles e auditorias para verificar se os modelos de IA estão funcionando conforme o planejado.
As medidas incluem avaliações internas, auditorias realizadas por uma empresa externa e análises pelos conselhos de administração de cada companhia.
Os executivos também concordaram em se reunir regularmente para estabelecer padrões e boas práticas com o objetivo de melhorar a segurança de seus sistemas.
A criação da Força da Superinteligência amplia a participação direta do governo estadunidense no debate sobre os riscos e a segurança dos sistemas de IA, ao mesmo tempo em que Trump busca garantir que os Estados Unidos mantenham a liderança no desenvolvimento da tecnologia.
Rodrigo Mozelli é jornalista formado pela Universidade Metodista de São Paulo (UMESP) e, atualmente, é redator do Olhar Digital.

articles.title: Zwei Jahre Warten, ein Ergebnis: Die neue Siri kann plötzlich mehr als Wecker stellen
articles.text:
Apples KI-Siri im Praxistest: Was sie auf dem Mac kann und woran sie noch scheitert
Statt im Sprint zur Konkurrenz aufzuholen, wurde die Geschichte um Siri AI für Apple zum Marathon. Mitte 2024 angekündigt, im Herbst 2026 mit den Updates auf iOS 27, macOS 27 und Co. erst fertig. Zu viel Arbeit musste man offenbar nachträglich investieren, zu wenig hat das Produkt intern überzeugt. Erst mithilfe von Google ist es dem iPhone-Unternehmen gelungen, eine verlässliche Version der KI-Siri zu entwickeln. Auf der WWDC 2026 wurde die Assistenz erneut vorgestellt. Diesmal soll sie funktionieren. Wie gut? Das haben wir im August 2026 mithilfe der Beta-Version von macOS 27 Golden Gate ausprobiert. Ihr könnt das auch – sogar in der EU.
So nutzt ihr Siri AI auf dem Mac
Apple hatte zwar im Rahmen der Entwicklerkonferenz angekündigt, die neue Siri-Version werde hierzulande zunächst nicht verfügbar sein. Das galt allerdings nur für das iPhone, denn beim Betriebssystem iOS und dem zugehörigen App-Store ist das Unternehmen als sogenannter Gatekeeper eingestuft. Hier müsste Apple Konkurrenten die gleichen Möglichkeiten einräumen, wie den eigenen Diensten.
Anders sieht es auf dem Mac aus. Hier wird Apple keine besondere Marktmacht zugeschrieben. Das Unternehmen kann Siri AI anbieten, ohne Sorge haben zu müssen, die nötigen Schnittstellen für andere öffnen zu müssen. Entsprechend lässt sich die neue KI-Assistenz schon jetzt ausprobieren, wenn man die nötigen Voraussetzungen erfüllt.
Dazu gehört ein kompatibler Apple-Computer. Zudem müsst ihr macOS 27 Golden Gate installiert haben. Die Systemsprache des Macs und die Sprache für Siri müssen auf US-Englisch eingestellt sein. Dabei ist zu beachten: Beta-Software kann immer Fehler enthalten und sollte nicht auf Arbeitsgeräte geladen werden. Verwendet im Idealfall ein zweites Macbook, das ihr nicht benötigt. Auch wir haben die Beta auf einem Test-Macbook installiert.
Ist die Installation geschafft, klickt ihr in den Einstellungen auf „Siri“ und dann auf „Try New Siri“. Im neuen Fenster klickt ihr auf „Join Waitlist“. Damit landet ihr auf einer Warteliste. Eine Notification verrät euch, wann ihr die neue Siri-Version nutzen könnt. Als wir das in der Entwickler-Beta ausprobiert haben, hat es nur wenige Minuten gedauert. Andere berichteten von längerer Wartezeit. Beeinflussen lässt sich der Vorgang nicht.
Was kann Siri AI auf dem Mac?
Ist alles erledigt, könnt ihr die neue Version von Siri auf drei Arten aktivieren. Wenn ihr die Spracherkennung eingerichtet habt, sagt ihr einfach „Siri“, ansonsten öffnet ihr mit CMD+Leertaste die Spotlightsuche, in die ihr eure Anfrage einfach eintippt. Alternativ klickt ihr aufs Mikrofon und sprecht eure Anfrage ein. Die dritte Möglichkeit ist die neue Siri-App im Dock. Bei den beiden letzteren Möglichkeiten könnt ihr entscheiden, ob ihr mit Siri sprechen oder euer Anliegen doch lieber einsprechen wollt. In den Siri-Einstellungen legt ihr zudem fest, ob die KI nur schriftlich oder auch akustisch antworten soll.
Danach könnt ihr Siri alles fragen. Und anders als früher erhaltet ihr in der Regel auch eine korrekte Antwort. Das Feld erstreckt sich weit. Von Fragen über Astronomie bis hin zur Tabelle der Formel‑1‑Weltmeisterschaft. Themen könnt ihr kontextbezogen vertiefen. Wer ist Erster in der Formel 1? Und wann hat Lewis Hamilton den ersten Sieg für Ferrari errungen? Diese Siri-Version kennt die richtige Antwort. Es ist auch möglich, die Assistenz Vergleiche anstellen zu lassen. Wir haben in unserem Beispiel etwa nach den Unterschieden zwischen dem höchsten Berg der Erde (Mount Everest) und dem des Mars (Olympus Mons) gefragt und eine ausführliche Antwort inklusive Vergleichstabelle erhalten. Auf Wunsch kann man solche Ergebnisse direkt per Sprachkommando als Notiz speichern.
Doch da geht noch mehr. Im Dialog mit der KI-Version ist in wenigen Minuten eine Urlaubsreise für die ganze Familie geplant, inklusive Kostenaufstellung, Erinnerung an den rechtzeitigen Fahrkartenkauf und Kalendereintrag für die Dauer des Urlaubs. Wie im Beispiel von der WWDC lässt sich der Trip auch so planen, dass man unterwegs noch Freunde besuchen kann. Der Zugriff auf die exklusiven Schnittstellen macht es möglich.
Im produktiven Einsatz kann Siri problemlos den Bildschirminhalt erkennen und so Artikel zusammenfassen oder eigene Texte erweitern, ohne dass ihr irgendwas davon in die Chatmaske posten müsst. Ein simpler Prompt genügt. Allerdings darf euch das Ergebnis dann nicht enttäuschen. Wir haben Siri zum Beispiel testweise gebeten, unseren Beitrag zu John Ternus als neuem Apple-CEO um einen Absatz zu Steve Jobs zu erweitern. Das hat die KI-Assistenz auch erledigt. Allerdings handelte es sich dabei eher um allgemeine Informationen, die Siri direkt unterm Text ergänzt hat, anstatt sie sinnvoll einzufügen.
Siri AI hat Grenzen
Aber Siri hat auch Grenzen. Jede ausprobierte Anfrage lief ohne WLAN-Verbindung ins Leere. Eine Internetverbindung war zumindest bei unserem Test Pflicht. Da stellt sich die Frage: Was passiert mit den Daten? Apple verspricht, diese durch das sogenannte Private Cloud Compute so gut wie möglich zu schützen. „Wenn Private Cloud Compute Nutzeranfragen verarbeitet, werden keine persönlichen Daten gespeichert, und weder Apple noch andere können darauf zugreifen“, heißt es dazu in der Ankündigung. Externe Entwickler:innen könnten dieses Versprechen jederzeit überprüfen. Außerdem laufen die Anfragen durch den sogenannten System-Orchestrator. Die Funktion koordiniert im Hintergrund, welche Schnittstellen Siri für die Anfrage verwenden muss. Dazu gehört etwa der lokale Index der Spotlight-Suche. Auch das dient dem Datenschutz.
Abseits davon ist die Funktion von Siri AI auf dem Mac beschränkt. Kalendereinträge, Notizen, Erinnerungen anlegen, das geht. Andere agentische Fähigkeiten hat Siri aber nicht. Die KI kann den Mac also nicht aufräumen, indem sie etwa im Downloads-Ordner alle PDFs in einen und alle Bilder in einen anderen Ordner sortiert.
Nichtsdestotrotz scheint es Apple diesmal wirklich gelungen zu sein, einen echten KI-Helfer in das System zu integrieren. Die Assistenz funktionierte schon in der Beta schon überraschend gut – wenn auch hauptsächlich nur auf Englisch. Allerdings muss die deutsche Lokalisierung nicht zwingend auf sich warten lassen. Wer den Chatbot bittet, auf Deutsch zu antworten, bekommt die Antworten zumindest auch schriftlich auf Deutsch. Und zwar zuverlässig und fehlerlos. Vielleicht dreht Apple hier also schnell nach dem Start nach.

articles.title: Amazon’s colorful and sturdy new Kindles
articles.text:
Hi, friends! Welcome to Installer No. 146, your guide to the best and Verge-iest stuff in the world. (If you’re new here, welcome, it’s October already?, and also you can read all the old editions at the Installer homepage.)
Amazon’s colorful and sturdy new Kindles
Plus, in this week’s Installer: OpenAI’s Dots, the remastered Witcher 3, Bose’s new wired earbuds, and more.
This week, I’m wishing I could do Walmart potato drone delivery in Portland, watching Mike Tomlin explain his incredible Minecraft city, pondering if the Gears of War pizza cutter is awesome or terrible, exploring Craig Mod’s walks, nodding along with MKBHD’s video about YouTube’s A/B video testing feature, hoping that more concerts ban phones, and celebrating soup season. It’s here!
Programming note: David is back next week! It’s been a blast writing Installer again, and thanks to everyone for reading and for your recommendations. For now, I also have for you Amazon’s new Kindles, OpenAI’s Dots, the remastered Witcher 3, and more.
(As always, the best part of Installer is your ideas and tips. What apps are you into right now? What are your favorite things you’ve watched / seen / zoned out to recently? Tell me everything: installer@theverge.com. And if you know someone else who might enjoy Installer, forward it to them and tell them to subscribe here.)
The Drop
- Amazon’s new Kindles. Amazon might have crushed it with the Kindle updates this year. The new base e-readers look like they’ll be a nice upgrade from previous generations, with flush front screens, an option for an aluminum back, and some nice new colors. The new Paperwhite and Colorsoft Signature Editions are compatible with a case with page turn buttons. And now there’s a “Kindle Click” remote to let you turn pages and adjust brightness. My years-old Paperwhite is still trucking along just fine, but if it suddenly broke, these would be really tempting options.
- OpenAI’s Dots. OpenAI’s Muse-like AI agent is here, though the company is pitching it more as something to help you with work than an all-encompassing assistant for your personal life. (That’s probably coming later.) The Dots are also adorable, though I think I’d give the Muse mascots the edge in cuteness.
- The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt — Remastered. Eleven years after its initial launch, The Witcher 3 is getting yet another big update. This free update for existing owners adds a lot of features and tweaks, including visual improvements, changes to skills, a new accessibility section in settings, cross-platform mod support, and more. The game is also now on Switch 2. Might be time for me to finally dive in.
- Bose’s Noise Cancelling Wired Earbuds. These $99 USB-C wired earbuds have noise cancellation and an in-line remote for adjusting volume with a built-in microphone for calls, and they come in three colors. As a huge fan of Apple’s wired EarPods, these could be a great option that’s a step above those in quality.
- Ace Combat 8: Wings of Theve. Bandai Namco’s latest entry in its fighter-pilot franchise sounds like a thrilling experience with a campaign filled with optimism, and it’s become one of the best-reviewed games of the year. Seems like a soaring success.
- Keurig’s Alta. The new Keurig coffee machine can make you a cup of joe with compostable pucks instead of the recyclable pods. Plus, it can also make espresso and looks super fancy. It’s not cheap at $499.99. But it’s tough to beat the convenience of a Keurig — I learned firsthand when my toddler was a newborn — so this could be a good option if you want to lead a Keurig life with more Earth-friendly pods.
- HP’s OmniBook 5 14. This HP laptop is thin and light, has 8GB of RAM, comes in good colors, and starts at $699.99, making it extremely MacBook Neo-adjacent. If you want the Neo ethos paired with Windows, this might be a solid option.
- Ikea’s Förlig lamp. This LED Ikea lamp lets you swap between 10 different colors, can be used from the floor or on a wall, and looks kind of like a lightsaber. Super fun.
Today I’m featuring Scott Stein, CNET’s editor at large. I’ve been a huge admirer of Stein’s work, especially his excellent coverage of wearables and VR, for years, and I had the great fortune of finally meeting him in person at Snap and Meta’s events last month.
I asked Scott to share his homescreen and the apps and things he cares about. Here it is, plus some info on the apps he uses and why:
The phone: I use an iPhone 16 Pro Max right now.
The apps: So I randomize my Home Screen apps. Madness? Maybe. I started doing it for fun by adding suggested Siri app widgets a few years ago. I add two of the widgets, 8 apps each, and then the bottom 8 are fixed ones plus the four on my dock.
My fixed ones are: Google Calendar, Photos, Notes, Camera, Music, Gmail, GMaps, Bluesky, Phone, Messages, Mail, Safari. My core go-tos.
But the others are a contextual-slash-frequency-based mix of things I might be using (or not). The locations shift. In some ways it’s like Home Screen gaslighting… but it’s also a living Black Mirror life, and often it’s actually helpful. Today there’s the United app since I’m flying, Uber, Siri, Voice Memos, Signal, GChat, YouTube, Asana, Yahoo Sports… mostly pretty useful.
The wallpaper: My background’s also randomized. I pull from family and trip photos so I can see my kids (and other odd moments) when I’m out and about. It comforts me.
I also asked Scott to share a few things he’s into right now. Here’s what he sent back:
The apps:
- I have had an ongoing magic hobby since I was a kid. I’m reading The Intuitive Magician: Mastering Magic Through Improvisation, by Justin Higham. Kind of technical but it’s an exploration of where practice and fluid improvising meet, which feels holistic for other things.
- Also reading Stephen King and Peter Straub’s Black House, after reading The Talisman. I loved the Dark Tower books and the new Talisman trilogy end is coming soon which apparently blends them all together.
- I’ve also been semi obsessed with runes lately, part of my interest in portable trinkets and talismans, and how readings can feel like a form of meditation.
- Still playing Fire Emblem: Fortune’s Weave, and carving out time ahead for Panic Playdate’s third season. I love that little handheld.
Crowdsourced
Here’s what the Installer community is into this week. I want to know what you’re into right now as well! Email installer@theverge.com with your recommendations for anything and everything, and we’ll feature some of our favorites here every week.
